title: Leviticus

stories.title: 🔥 Leviticus 1
summaryBullets: Then the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting, saying, (1:1).
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them: When any of you brings an offering to the LORD, you may bring as your offering an animal from the herd or the flock. (1:2).
If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he is to present an unblemished male. He must bring it to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for its acceptance before the LORD. (1:3).
He is to lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him. (1:4).
And he shall slaughter the young bull before the LORD, and Aaron’s sons the priests are to present the blood and splatter it on all sides of the altar at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (1:5).
Next, he is to skin the burnt offering and cut it into pieces. (1:6).
The sons of Aaron the priest shall put a fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire. (1:7).
Then Aaron’s sons the priests are to arrange the pieces, including the head and the fat, atop the burning wood on the altar. (1:8).
The entrails and legs must be washed with water, and the priest shall burn all of it on the altar as a burnt offering, a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (1:9).
If, however, one’s offering is a burnt offering from the flock — from the sheep or goats — he is to present an unblemished male. (1:10).
He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar before the LORD, and Aaron’s sons the priests are to splatter its blood against the altar on all sides. (1:11).
He is to cut the animal into pieces, and the priest shall arrange them, including the head and fat, atop the burning wood that is on the altar. (1:12).
The entrails and legs must be washed with water, and the priest shall present all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (1:13).
If, instead, one’s offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, he is to present a turtledove or a young pigeon. (1:14).
Then the priest shall bring it to the altar, twist off its head, and burn it on the altar; its blood should be drained out on the side of the altar. (1:15).
And he is to remove the crop with its contents and throw it to the east side of the altar, in the place for ashes. (1:16).

He shall tear it open by its wings, without dividing the bird completely. And the priest is to burn it on the altar atop the burning wood. It is a burnt offering, a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (1:17).
crossRefs: Genesis 8:20-21: Noah's burnt offering after the flood, and the LORD smelling the pleasing aroma.
Genesis 22:2-13: Abraham is sent to offer a burnt offering, and a ram caught in a thicket is offered instead of Isaac.
Leviticus 6:8-13: The priests' law for the burnt offering, and the fire on the altar that must never go out.
Numbers 28:1-8: The morning and evening burnt offering fixed as a daily obligation for the nation.
Luke 2:24: A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons offered, the provision this chapter makes for the poor.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּפֶּר (kipper), to cover or to wipe clean - Greek (LXX): ἐξιλάσκομαι (exilaskomai)
translationNotes.note: The verb's first use in this book is at 1:4, where laying a hand on the burnt offering makes it acceptable to make atonement for the man. Kipper carries the senses of covering over and of wiping away; the related noun kapporet names the gold lid of the ark (Exodus 25:17). Leviticus 17:11 gives the mechanism the book works on, that the blood makes atonement by the life in it, and the whole of Leviticus 16 is built around the word.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סָמַךְ (samakh), to lean or press down
translationNotes.note: Samakh is not a light touch; it is leaning your weight on something. The offerer presses his hand on the head of the animal at 1:4, and the same act is repeated for the peace offering (3:2) and the sin offering (4:4). Leviticus 16:21 shows what it means: Aaron leans both hands on the live goat and confesses Israel's sins over it. The gesture identifies whose offering this is and what it stands in for.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִקְטִיר (hiqtir), from a root meaning to send up smoke
translationNotes.note: A different verb from ordinary burning. Saraph is what you do to rubbish and to the parts taken outside the camp (4:12); hiqtir is what happens on the altar, where the portion goes up as smoke. English usually flattens both to 'burn,' so the reader cannot see that Leviticus is using two words for two different acts in the same chapter.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹלָה (olah), 'that which goes up' - Greek: ὁλοκαύτωμα (holokautoma), 'wholly burned'
translationNotes.note: The one offering burned entire, with nothing left for the worshiper to eat. The Hebrew name describes the smoke going up; the Greek name, which gives English 'holocaust,' describes the whole animal burning. Leviticus 7:8 leaves the priest only the hide, so this was the costliest offering a man could bring.

Leviticus 1 grades the burnt offering by means: a bull from the herd, a ram or male goat from the flock, or a turtledove or young pigeon. A bull was a working animal and a year's plough power; a bird could be caught. The graded list runs through the whole book, so that nobody was priced out of coming.

Built on the verb nuach, to rest or settle, so the sense is a soothing or restful smell. The phrase first appears at Noah's offering in Genesis 8:21 and runs through Leviticus as the standard formula for an accepted sacrifice. Ephesians 5:2 takes the phrase up in Greek.

Older English versions render this 'offering made by fire,' which is closer to the Hebrew than 'food offering.' It marks any portion put on the altar and consumed in the flame. Leviticus 3:11 calls the burned portion 'food,' which is why some translations use that word here.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Lord instructs Moses on burnt offerings: animals from the herd or flock must be male and without defect, presented at the tent of meeting where the offerer lays a hand on it before slaughter, and the priest burns the pieces on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. Birds may be offered as an alternative, with specific instructions for preparation.

stories.title: 🔥 Leviticus 2
summaryBullets: “When anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD, his offering must consist of fine flour. He is to pour olive oil on it, put frankincense on it, (2:1).

and bring it to Aaron’s sons the priests. The priest shall take a handful of the flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and burn this as a memorial portion on the altar, a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (2:2).
The remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD. (2:3).
Now if you bring an offering of grain baked in an oven, it must consist of fine flour, either unleavened cakes mixed with oil or unleavened wafers coated with oil. (2:4).
If your offering is a grain offering prepared on a griddle, it must be unleavened bread made of fine flour mixed with oil. (2:5).
Crumble it and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering. (2:6).
If your offering is a grain offering cooked in a pan, it must consist of fine flour with oil. (2:7).
When you bring to the LORD the grain offering made in any of these ways, it is to be presented to the priest, and he shall take it to the altar. (2:8).
The priest is to remove the memorial portion from the grain offering and burn it on the altar as a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (2:9).
But the remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD. (2:10).
No grain offering that you present to the LORD may be made with leaven, for you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD. (2:11).
You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma. (2:12).
And you shall season each of your grain offerings with salt. You must not leave the salt of the covenant of your God out of your grain offering; you are to add salt to each of your offerings. (2:13).
If you bring a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire. (2:14).
And you are to put oil and frankincense on it; it is a grain offering. (2:15).
The priest shall then burn the memorial portion of the crushed grain and the oil, together with all its frankincense, as a food offering to the LORD. (2:16).
crossRefs: Leviticus 6:14-23: The priests' law for the grain offering and the share they eat in the courtyard.
Leviticus 24:5-9: Twelve loaves of fine flour with frankincense, set out on the gold table every Sabbath.
Numbers 15:1-12: The measures of flour, oil, and wine that accompany each kind of animal offering.
Numbers 18:19: The priests' portions given as a permanent covenant of salt before the LORD.
Numbers 5:15: A grain offering brought without oil or frankincense, in a case of suspicion.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים (qodesh qodashim), literally 'holy of holies'
translationNotes.note: A Hebrew way of forming a superlative by doubling the noun, the same construction as 'king of kings' and 'song of songs.' It marks a top grade of holiness with practical rules attached: what is most holy may be eaten only by male priests and only in a holy place (6:16-18, 7:6). The same phrase names the innermost room of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:33), and 2:3 applies it to the priests' share of the grain offering.

The first portion of each harvest offered to God before the rest could be eaten (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:9-14). Paul calls the resurrected Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20); the guarantee that the full resurrection harvest will follow.

A milky-white resin from the Boswellia tree of southern Arabia. Burned as incense in the temple (Exodus 30:34); offered with every grain offering. The magi's second gift, traditionally read as signaling priesthood.

The only prescribed offering with no blood and no animal: fine flour, olive oil, and frankincense, raw or baked. Minchah is the ordinary word for the tribute a subject brings his king, as in Judges 3:15. A handful goes on the altar and the rest feeds the priests (2:3).

Not ordinary meal but the finest sifted wheat flour, the grade a household would keep for guests; Genesis 18:6 has Abraham calling for it when three visitors arrive. Grinding it by hand and sifting it took real work, which is part of what the offering cost.

Salt does not spoil and does not change, which is why an agreement sealed with it was called a covenant of salt. Numbers 18:19 uses the phrase for the priests' portions, and 2 Chronicles 13:5 for the throne given to David's line. Leviticus 2:13 requires it on every offering.

The handful of flour, oil, and all of the frankincense that goes up in smoke while the rest of the offering stays with the priests. It stands for the whole gift. Acts 10:4 uses the same idea in Greek of Cornelius' prayers and gifts going up as a memorial.

stories.keyTakeaway: Grain offerings to the Lord are made from finest flour with oil and incense; a memorial portion is burned on the altar while the rest goes to Aaron and his sons, with variations allowed for oven-baked, griddle, or pan-cooked preparations, all made without yeast and seasoned with salt.

stories.title: 🔥 Leviticus 3
summaryBullets: “If one’s offering is a peace offering and he offers an animal from the herd, whether male or female, he must present it without blemish before the LORD. (3:1).
He is to lay his hand on the head of the offering and slaughter it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. Then Aaron’s sons the priests shall splatter the blood on all sides of the altar. (3:2).
From the peace offering he is to bring a food offering to the LORD: the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them, (3:3).
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys. (3:4).
Then Aaron’s sons are to burn it on the altar atop the burnt offering that is on the burning wood, as a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (3:5).
If, however, one’s peace offering to the LORD is from the flock, he must present a male or female without blemish. (3:6).
If he is presenting a lamb for his offering, he must present it before the LORD. (3:7).
He is to lay his hand on the head of his offering and slaughter it in front of the Tent of Meeting. Then Aaron’s sons shall splatter its blood on all sides of the altar. (3:8).

And from the peace offering he shall bring a food offering to the LORD consisting of its fat: the entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone, the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them, (3:9).
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys. (3:10).
Then the priest is to burn them on the altar as food, a food offering to the LORD. (3:11).
If one’s offering is a goat, he is to present it before the LORD. (3:12).
He must lay his hand on its head and slaughter it in front of the Tent of Meeting. Then Aaron’s sons shall splatter its blood on all sides of the altar. (3:13).
And from his offering he shall present a food offering to the LORD: the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them, (3:14).
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys. (3:15).
Then the priest is to burn the food on the altar as a food offering, a pleasing aroma. All the fat is the LORD’s. (3:16).
This is a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live: You must not eat any fat or any blood.” (3:17).
crossRefs: Leviticus 7:11-21: The three kinds of peace offering and how long the meat may be kept.
Leviticus 7:28-34: The breast and the right thigh set aside from every peace offering for the priests.
Leviticus 17:10-14: The blood is never eaten; it is given on the altar to make atonement.
Deuteronomy 12:17-18: These offerings are eaten before the LORD at the place He chooses, with your household.
1 Samuel 1:3-9: Elkanah's yearly sacrifice at Shiloh, with portions handed round to his family.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זֶבַח שְׁלָמִים (zevach shelamim), from שָׁלוֹם (shalom)
translationNotes.note: The only offering the worshiper himself ate. God received the fat and the blood, the priest received the breast and the right thigh (Leviticus 7:31-34), and the rest went home as a meal for the family and guests. It is a shared feast, which is why it is also rendered fellowship offering.

Not the marbling in the meat but the hard suet around the entrails, kidneys, and liver, plus the fat tail of the local sheep, which on a fat-tailed breed can weigh several pounds by itself. Leviticus 3:16 assigns all of it to the LORD, and 3:17 forbids Israel to eat any of it.

A formula that lifts a command out of the tabernacle and puts it in every household, in the camp or later in the land. It appears on the fat and blood rule here, on the Sabbath in Leviticus 23:3, and on the feasts in Leviticus 23:14 and 23:21.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זָכָר אוֹ נְקֵבָה תָּמִים (zakhar o neqevah tamim)
translationNotes.note: The peace offering is the only one that may be either sex (3:1, 3:6); the burnt offering and the leader's sin offering both require a male (1:3, 4:23). Tamim means whole or sound rather than morally perfect, and Leviticus 22:22-24 lists what disqualifies an animal: blindness, an injury, a wart, a running sore, a crushed or torn part. The rule is that the animal given up must be one that was worth keeping.

stories.keyTakeaway: Instructions are given for fellowship offerings from the herd, flock, or goats; the offerer lays a hand on the animal's head, it is slaughtered, and the priests burn the fat and organs on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD. A lasting ordinance forbids eating fat or blood.

stories.title: 🔥 Leviticus 4
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (4:1).
“Tell the Israelites to do as follows with one who sins unintentionally against any of the LORD’s commandments and does what is forbidden by them: (4:2).
If the anointed priest sins, bringing guilt on the people, he must bring to the LORD a young bull without blemish as a sin offering for the sin he has committed. (4:3).
He must bring the bull to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD, lay his hand on the bull’s head, and slaughter it before the LORD. (4:4).
Then the anointed priest shall take some of the bull’s blood and bring it into the Tent of Meeting. (4:5).
The priest is to dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of it seven times before the LORD, in front of the veil of the sanctuary. (4:6).

The priest must then put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense that is before the LORD in the Tent of Meeting. And he is to pour out the rest of the bull’s blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (4:7).
Then he shall remove all the fat from the bull of the sin offering— the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them, (4:8).
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys— (4:9).
just as the fat is removed from the ox of the peace offering. Then the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering. (4:10).
But the hide of the bull and all its flesh, with its head and legs and its entrails and dung— (4:11).
all the rest of the bull— he must take outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place where the ashes are poured out, and there he must burn it on a wood fire on the ash heap. (4:12).

Now if the whole congregation of Israel strays unintentionally and the matter escapes the notice of the assembly so that they violate any of the LORD’s commandments and incur guilt by doing what is forbidden, (4:13).
when they become aware of the sin they have committed, then the assembly must bring a young bull as a sin offering and present it before the Tent of Meeting. (4:14).
The elders of the congregation are to lay their hands on the bull’s head before the LORD, and it shall be slaughtered before the LORD. (4:15).
Then the anointed priest is to bring some of the bull’s blood into the Tent of Meeting, (4:16).
and he is to dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD in front of the veil. (4:17).

He is also to put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is before the LORD in the Tent of Meeting, and he must pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (4:18).
And he is to remove all the fat from it and burn it on the altar. (4:19).
He shall offer this bull just as he did the bull for the sin offering; in this way the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven. (4:20).
Then he is to take the bull outside the camp and burn it, just as he burned the first bull. It is the sin offering for the assembly. (4:21).
When a leader sins unintentionally and does what is prohibited by any of the commandments of the LORD his God, he incurs guilt. (4:22).
When he becomes aware of the sin he has committed, he must bring an unblemished male goat as his offering. (4:23).
He is to lay his hand on the head of the goat and slaughter it at the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered before the LORD. It is a sin offering. (4:24).

Then the priest is to take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. (4:25).
He must burn all its fat on the altar, like the fat of the peace offerings; thus the priest will make atonement for that man’s sin, and he will be forgiven. (4:26).
And if one of the common people sins unintentionally and does what is prohibited by any of the LORD’s commandments, he incurs guilt. (4:27).
When he becomes aware of the sin he has committed, he must bring an unblemished female goat as his offering for that sin. (4:28).
He is to lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and slaughter it at the place of the burnt offering. (4:29).
Then the priest is to take some of its blood with his finger, put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. (4:30).

Then he is to remove all the fat, just as it is removed from the peace offering, and the priest is to burn it on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD. In this way the priest will make atonement for him, and he will be forgiven. (4:31).
If, however, he brings a lamb as a sin offering, he must bring an unblemished female. (4:32).
And he is to lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and slaughter it as a sin offering at the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered. (4:33).

Then the priest is to take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and pour out the rest of its blood at the base of the altar. (4:34).

And he shall remove all the fat, just as the fat of the lamb is removed from the peace offerings, and he shall burn it on the altar along with the food offerings to the LORD. In this way the priest will make atonement for him for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven. (4:35).
crossRefs: Numbers 15:22-31: The line drawn between sin committed unintentionally and sin committed with a high hand.
Leviticus 6:24-30: The priests' law for the sin offering, where it is eaten, and when it must be burned instead.
Leviticus 16:11-19: The high priest carries sin offering blood behind the veil on the Day of Atonement.
Hebrews 13:11-12: The bodies of the animals whose blood is taken into the sanctuary are burned outside the camp.
Psalm 19:12: Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַטָּאת (chattat) - the verb חִטֵּא (chitte), 'to de-sin, to purify'
translationNotes.note: The noun is the same word as 'sin,' but the related verb means to remove sin, so this offering is a purification rite as much as a penalty. Its blood is put on the horns of the altar and, for the gravest cases, carried inside the tent. Leviticus 4 cleanses the sanctuary as well as the sinner.

The whole chapter is about sin committed without meaning to, discovered afterward. Numbers 15:30 sets the boundary: sin committed with a high hand has no offering prescribed. Leviticus 4 assumes a man can be guilty of something he did not know he was doing.

The offering rises with the offender's standing. The anointed priest and the whole congregation each bring a bull; a leader brings a male goat; an ordinary person brings a female goat or a lamb (4:3, 4:14, 4:23, 4:28). The higher the office, the heavier the cost of getting it wrong.

When the sin offering is for the anointed priest or for the whole congregation, its blood goes inside the tent and the rest of the carcass is carried out of the camp and burned on a wood fire at the place where the ashes are dumped (4:11-12, 4:21). No one eats any of it. Hebrews 13:11-13 builds directly on this rule, noting that the bodies of those animals are burned outside the camp and that Jesus suffered outside the gate.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses on sin offerings for unintentional violations of his commands, prescribing different animals and procedures depending on whether the anointed priest, the whole community, a leader, or an ordinary member sins.

stories.title: 🔥 Leviticus 5
summaryBullets: “If someone sins by failing to testify when he hears a public charge about something he has witnessed, whether he has seen it or learned of it, he shall bear the iniquity. (5:1).
Or if a person touches anything unclean— whether the carcass of any unclean wild animal or livestock or crawling creature— even if he is unaware of it, he is unclean and guilty. (5:2).
Or if he touches human uncleanness— anything by which one becomes unclean— even if he is unaware of it, when he realizes it, he is guilty. (5:3).

Or if someone swears thoughtlessly with his lips to do anything good or evil— in whatever matter a man may rashly pronounce an oath— even if he is unaware of it, when he realizes it, he is guilty in the matter. (5:4).
If someone incurs guilt in one of these ways, he must confess the sin he has committed, (5:5).

and he must bring his guilt offering to the LORD for the sin he has committed: a female lamb or goat from the flock as a sin offering. And the priest will make atonement for him concerning his sin. (5:6).
If, however, he cannot afford a lamb, he may bring to the LORD as restitution for his sin two turtledoves or two young pigeons — one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering. (5:7).
He is to bring them to the priest, who shall first present the one for the sin offering. He is to twist its head at the front of its neck without severing it; (5:8).
then he is to sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar, while the rest of the blood is drained out at the base of the altar. It is a sin offering. (5:9).

And the priest must prepare the second bird as a burnt offering according to the ordinance. In this way the priest will make atonement for him for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven. (5:10).

But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he may bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a sin offering. He must not put olive oil or frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering. (5:11).
He is to bring it to the priest, who shall take a handful from it as a memorial portion and burn it on the altar atop the food offerings to the LORD; it is a sin offering. (5:12).
In this way the priest will make atonement for him for any of these sins he has committed, and he will be forgiven. The remainder will belong to the priest, like the grain offering.” (5:13).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (5:14).

“If someone acts unfaithfully and sins unintentionally against any of the LORD’s holy things, he must bring his guilt offering to the LORD: an unblemished ram from the flock, of proper value in silver shekels according to the sanctuary shekel; it is a guilt offering. (5:15).

Regarding any holy thing he has harmed, he must make restitution by adding a fifth of its value to it and giving it to the priest, who will make atonement on his behalf with the ram as a guilt offering, and he will be forgiven. (5:16).
If someone sins and violates any of the LORD’s commandments even though he was unaware, he is guilty and shall bear his punishment. (5:17).

He is to bring to the priest an unblemished ram of proper value from the flock as a guilt offering. Then the priest will make atonement on his behalf for the wrong he has committed in ignorance, and he will be forgiven. (5:18).
It is a guilt offering; he was certainly guilty before the LORD.” (5:19).
crossRefs: Leviticus 6:1-7: The guilt offering for property taken by deceit, with restitution and a fifth added.
Leviticus 12:8: The same concession for the poor, two turtledoves or two young pigeons instead of a lamb.
Numbers 5:5-8: Confession, full restitution with a fifth added, paid to the wronged man or his kinsman.
Leviticus 27:1-8: Valuations in sanctuary shekels, with a reduced assessment set by the priest for the poor.
Isaiah 53:10: The LORD makes His life a guilt offering.

translationNotes.note: The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).

A milky-white resin from the Boswellia tree of southern Arabia. Burned as incense in the temple (Exodus 30:34); offered with every grain offering. The magi's second gift, traditionally read as signaling priesthood.

Both a weight (about 0.4 oz / 11 g) and a currency unit. In Old Testament economy a common laborer earned roughly half a shekel per month, so the 20 shekels paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28) was about three years of wages. The temple tax was half a shekel (Exodus 30:13); in New Testament reckoning that equaled two denarii / two days' wages.

This offering settles a debt as well as a sin. Where property or holy things are involved the offender repays the value, adds a fifth on top, and then brings a ram (5:15-16; 6:4-6). The ram is assessed in silver by the sanctuary standard, so the offering could not be dodged with a cheap animal.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְאִם־לֹא תַגִּיעַ יָדוֹ (ve-im lo taggia yado), 'if his hand does not reach'
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew idiom is about reach, not intent. Leviticus 5:7-13 steps the sin offering down twice: a lamb, then two birds, then a tenth of an ephah of plain flour, about two quarts. The flour version carries no oil and no frankincense, so it costs the poorest man the least the system can accept and still counts as atonement.

translationNotes.term: of proper value in silver shekels
translationNotes.note: The animal has to meet an assessed silver value by the sanctuary shekel of about 11.4 grams. Leviticus 27 gives the schedule of such valuations, and Leviticus 27:25 fixes the standard at twenty gerahs to the shekel. This is a priced obligation, not a gesture.

stories.keyTakeaway: Laws are given for unintentional sins: silence during testimony, touching unclean things, careless oaths, and violations of holy things; offerings vary by ability - a female lamb or goat, two doves or pigeons, or fine flour - with the priest making atonement. Those who sin against the Lord's commands unknowingly must bring a ram as a guilt offering, make restitution plus a fifth penalty, and receive forgiveness through the priest's atonement.

stories.title: 🔥 Leviticus 6
summaryBullets: And the LORD said to Moses, (6:1).
“If someone sins and acts unfaithfully against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in regard to a deposit or security entrusted to him or stolen, or if he extorts his neighbor (6:2).
or finds lost property and lies about it and swears falsely, or if he commits any such sin that a man might commit— (6:3).
once he has sinned and becomes guilty, he must return what he has stolen or taken by extortion, or the deposit entrusted to him, or the lost property he found, (6:4).
or anything else about which he has sworn falsely. He must make restitution in full, add a fifth of the value, and pay it to the owner on the day he acknowledges his guilt. (6:5).
Then he must bring to the priest his guilt offering to the LORD: an unblemished ram of proper value from the flock. (6:6).
In this way the priest will make atonement for him before the LORD, and he will be forgiven for anything he may have done to incur guilt.” (6:7).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (6:8).

“Command Aaron and his sons that this is the law of the burnt offering: The burnt offering is to remain on the hearth of the altar all night, until morning, and the fire must be kept burning on the altar. (6:9).
And the priest shall put on his linen robe and linen undergarments, and he shall remove from the altar the ashes of the burnt offering that the fire has consumed and place them beside it. (6:10).
Then he must take off his garments, put on other clothes, and carry the ashes outside the camp to a ceremonially clean place. (6:11).

The fire on the altar shall be kept burning; it must not be extinguished. Every morning the priest is to add wood to the fire, arrange the burnt offering on it, and burn the fat portions of the peace offerings on it. (6:12).
The fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it must not be extinguished. (6:13).
Now this is the law of the grain offering: Aaron’s sons shall present it before the LORD in front of the altar. (6:14).

The priest is to remove a handful of fine flour and olive oil, together with all the frankincense from the grain offering, and burn the memorial portion on the altar as a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (6:15).
Aaron and his sons are to eat the remainder. It must be eaten without leaven in a holy place; they are to eat it in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. (6:16).
It must not be baked with leaven; I have assigned it as their portion of My food offerings. It is most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering. (6:17).
Any male among the sons of Aaron may eat it. This is a permanent portion from the food offerings to the LORD for the generations to come. Anything that touches them will become holy.” (6:18).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (6:19).

“This is the offering that Aaron and his sons must present to the LORD on the day he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half in the evening. (6:20).
It shall be prepared with oil on a griddle; you are to bring it well-kneaded and present it as a grain offering broken in pieces, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (6:21).
The priest, who is one of Aaron’s sons and will be anointed to take his place, is to prepare it. As a permanent portion for the LORD, it must be burned completely. (6:22).
Every grain offering for a priest shall be burned completely; it is not to be eaten.” (6:23).
And the LORD said to Moses, (6:24).

“Tell Aaron and his sons that this is the law of the sin offering: In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, the sin offering shall be slaughtered before the LORD; it is most holy. (6:25).
The priest who offers it shall eat it; it must be eaten in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. (6:26).
Anything that touches its flesh will become holy, and if any of the blood is spattered on a garment, you must wash it in a holy place. (6:27).
The clay pot in which the sin offering is boiled must be broken; if it is boiled in a bronze pot, the pot must be scoured and rinsed with water. (6:28).
Any male among the priests may eat it; it is most holy. (6:29).
But no sin offering may be eaten if its blood has been brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it must be burned. (6:30).
crossRefs: Exodus 22:7-9: The law on a deposit stolen from a neighbor's house, and both parties brought before the judges.
Numbers 5:5-8: The wrong confessed, the loss repaid in full with a fifth added.
Exodus 27:20-21: Pure pressed oil brought so the lamps burn from evening until morning as a permanent statute.
Leviticus 10:12-15: Aaron's sons told exactly where and how to eat their share of the offerings.
Luke 19:8: Zacchaeus promises to repay fourfold anything he has taken by fraud.

translationNotes.note: The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).

A milky-white resin from the Boswellia tree of southern Arabia. Burned as incense in the temple (Exodus 30:34); offered with every grain offering. The magi's second gift, traditionally read as signaling priesthood.

A flat twenty percent added on top of full restitution, paid to the person wronged on the day the offender admits it (6:5). The same surcharge attaches to redeeming anything dedicated to God (Leviticus 27:13, 27:15, 27:19). It makes owning up cost more than being caught would have.

translationNotes.term: the fire must not go out
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵשׁ תָּמִיד (esh tamid), 'a continual fire'
translationNotes.note: The command is repeated three times in five verses (6:9, 6:12, 6:13). Wood had to be carried and added every morning, in a wilderness with almost no timber, which made keeping the fire a daily standing duty. Nehemiah 10:34 records lots being cast over who would supply the wood.

Plain linen, not the gold-worked garments of Exodus 28. The priest wore it to carry ashes off the altar, then changed clothes before going outside the camp (6:10-11). Holy dress stayed inside the sanctuary; the same rule puts the high priest in plain linen on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:4).

stories.keyTakeaway: When someone deceives a neighbor or swears falsely, they must return what they took or found, add a fifth of its value, and bring a guilt offering to be forgiven. The chapter then details regulations for the burnt offering, grain offering, the anointed priest's grain offering, and the sin offering, specifying how priests are to handle each sacrifice.

stories.title: 🔥 Leviticus 7
summaryBullets: “Now this is the law of the guilt offering, which is most holy: (7:1).
The guilt offering must be slaughtered in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, and the priest shall splatter its blood on all sides of the altar. (7:2).
And all the fat from it shall be offered: the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails, (7:3).
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which is to be removed with the kidneys. (7:4).
The priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering to the LORD; it is a guilt offering. (7:5).
Every male among the priests may eat of it. It must be eaten in a holy place; it is most holy. (7:6).
The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both. It belongs to the priest who makes atonement with it. (7:7).
As for the priest who presents a burnt offering for anyone, the hide of that offering belongs to him. (7:8).
Likewise , every grain offering that is baked in an oven or cooked in a pan or on a griddle belongs to the priest who presents it, (7:9).
and every grain offering, whether dry or mixed with oil, belongs equally to all the sons of Aaron. (7:10).
Now this is the law of the peace offering that one may present to the LORD: (7:11).

If he offers it in thanksgiving, then along with the sacrifice of thanksgiving he shall offer unleavened cakes mixed with olive oil, unleavened wafers coated with oil, and well-kneaded cakes of fine flour mixed with oil. (7:12).
Along with his peace offering of thanksgiving he is to present an offering with cakes of leavened bread. (7:13).
From the cakes he must present one portion of each offering as a contribution to the LORD. It belongs to the priest who sprinkles the blood of the peace offering. (7:14).
The meat of the sacrifice of his peace offering of thanksgiving must be eaten on the day he offers it; none of it may be left until morning. (7:15).
If, however, the sacrifice he offers is a vow or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day he presents his sacrifice, but the remainder may be eaten on the next day. (7:16).
But any meat of the sacrifice remaining until the third day must be burned up. (7:17).

If any of the meat from his peace offering is eaten on the third day, it will not be accepted. It will not be credited to the one who presented it; it shall be an abomination, and the one who eats of it shall bear his iniquity. (7:18).
Meat that touches anything unclean must not be eaten; it is to be burned up. As for any other meat, anyone who is ceremonially clean may eat it. (7:19).
But if anyone who is unclean eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people. (7:20).

If one touches anything unclean, whether human uncleanness, an unclean animal, or any unclean, detestable thing, and then eats any of the meat of the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people.” (7:21).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (7:22).
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘You are not to eat any of the fat of an ox, a sheep, or a goat. (7:23).
The fat of an animal found dead or mauled by wild beasts may be used for any other purpose, but you must not eat it. (7:24).
If anyone eats the fat of an animal from which a food offering may be presented to the LORD, the one who eats it must be cut off from his people. (7:25).
You must not eat the blood of any bird or animal in any of your dwellings. (7:26).
If anyone eats blood, that person must be cut off from his people.’” (7:27).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (7:28).
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘Anyone who presents a peace offering to the LORD must bring it as his sacrifice to the LORD. (7:29).
With his own hands he is to bring the food offerings to the LORD; he shall bring the fat, together with the breast, and wave the breast as a wave offering before the LORD. (7:30).
The priest is to burn the fat on the altar, but the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons. (7:31).
And you are to give the right thigh to the priest as a contribution from your peace offering. (7:32).
The son of Aaron who presents the blood and fat of the peace offering shall have the right thigh as a portion. (7:33).

I have taken from the sons of Israel the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution of their peace offerings, and I have given them to Aaron the priest and his sons as a permanent portion from the sons of Israel.’” (7:34).
This is the portion of the food offerings to the LORD for Aaron and his sons since the day they were presented to serve the LORD as priests. (7:35).
On the day they were anointed, the LORD commanded that this be given them by the sons of Israel. It is a permanent portion for the generations to come. (7:36).
This is the law of the burnt offering, the grain offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the ordination offering, and the peace offering, (7:37).
which the LORD gave Moses on Mount Sinai on the day He commanded the Israelites to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai. (7:38).
crossRefs: Leviticus 3:1-17: The peace offering and the fat portions burned to the LORD.
Exodus 29:26-28: The breast and the thigh first assigned to Aaron and his sons at their ordination.
Deuteronomy 18:1-5: The priests' portion from the people's sacrifices, since Levi has no inheritance of land.
1 Samuel 2:12-17: Eli's sons seize the meat before the fat is burned and treat the offering with contempt.
1 Corinthians 9:13-14: Those who serve at the altar share in what is offered on the altar.

translationNotes.note: Leviticus 7:22-27 forbids eating either, and the penalty for both is being cut off from the people. The fat meant is the hard suet packed around the kidneys and entrails, the part that burns best and was reckoned the choicest, which is why it goes to God (3:16). The ban on blood is grounded at 17:11, that the life is in the blood and it is given for atonement; Acts 15:20 keeps the same restriction for Gentile believers.

One of three kinds of peace offering, alongside a vow offering and a freewill offering. The thank offering has the shortest window: it must be eaten the same day (7:15), while the other two may run to the second day. Psalm 116:17 and Psalm 50:14 use todah for the sacrifice and for the praise together.

translationNotes.term: the hide belongs to the priest
translationNotes.note: Everything else in a burnt offering goes up in smoke, so the skin is the priest's only material return from it (7:8). Leather was valuable and durable, and this one line is what paid the priesthood from the most common sacrifice in Israel.

A narrow technical word, not the general term for what is detestable. Piggul means sacrificial meat that has gone past its allowed time and so is refused, and it occurs only four times in the Hebrew Bible. Leviticus 7:18 applies it to peace offering meat eaten on the third day.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses on the regulations for guilt offerings, fellowship offerings, and related sacrifices, including which parts priests may eat, how long meat may be kept, and prohibitions against eating fat and blood. He also specifies the portions of offerings that belong to Aaron and his sons as their perpetual share.

stories.title: 🩸 Leviticus 8
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (8:1).
“Take Aaron and his sons, their garments, the anointing oil, the bull of the sin offering, the two rams, and the basket of unleavened bread, (8:2).
and assemble the whole congregation at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” (8:3).
So Moses did as the LORD had commanded him, and the assembly gathered at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (8:4).
And Moses said to them, “This is what the LORD has commanded to be done.” (8:5).
Then Moses presented Aaron and his sons and washed them with water. (8:6).
He put the tunic on Aaron, tied the sash around him, clothed him with the robe, and put the ephod on him. He tied the woven band of the ephod around him and fastened it to him. (8:7).
Then he put the breastpiece on him and placed the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece. (8:8).
Moses also put the turban on Aaron’s head and set the gold plate, the holy diadem, on the front of the turban, as the LORD had commanded him. (8:9).
Next, Moses took the anointing oil and anointed the tabernacle and everything in it; and so he consecrated them. (8:10).
He sprinkled some of the oil on the altar seven times, anointing the altar and all its utensils, and the basin with its stand, to consecrate them. (8:11).
He also poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron’s head and anointed him to consecrate him. (8:12).
Then Moses presented Aaron’s sons, put tunics on them, wrapped sashes around them, and tied headbands on them, just as the LORD had commanded him. (8:13).
Moses then brought the bull near for the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. (8:14).

Moses slaughtered the bull, took some of the blood, and applied it with his finger to all four horns of the altar, purifying the altar. He poured out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar and consecrated it so that atonement could be made on it. (8:15).
Moses also took all the fat that was on the entrails, the lobe of the liver, and both kidneys and their fat, and burned it all on the altar. (8:16).
But the bull with its hide, flesh, and dung he burned outside the camp, as the LORD had commanded him. (8:17).
Then Moses presented the ram for the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. (8:18).
Moses slaughtered the ram and splattered the blood on all sides of the altar. (8:19).
He cut the ram into pieces and burned the head, the pieces, and the fat. (8:20).
He washed the entrails and legs with water and burned the entire ram on the altar as a burnt offering, a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. (8:21).
After that, Moses presented the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. (8:22).
Moses slaughtered the ram and took some of its blood and put it on Aaron’s right earlobe, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot. (8:23).

Moses also presented Aaron’s sons and put some of the blood on their right earlobes, on the thumbs of their right hands, and on the big toes of their right feet. Then he splattered the blood on all sides of the altar. (8:24).
And Moses took the fat— the fat tail, all the fat that was on the entrails, the lobe of the liver, and both kidneys with their fat— as well as the right thigh. (8:25).

And from the basket of unleavened bread that was before the LORD, he took one cake of unleavened bread, one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer, and he placed them on the fat portions and on the right thigh. (8:26).
He put all these in the hands of Aaron and his sons and waved them before the LORD as a wave offering. (8:27).
Then Moses took these from their hands and burned them on the altar with the burnt offering. This was an ordination offering, a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. (8:28).
He also took the breast — Moses’ portion of the ram of ordination — and waved it before the LORD as a wave offering, as the LORD had commanded him. (8:29).

Next, Moses took some of the anointing oil and some of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled them on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and their garments. So he consecrated Aaron and his garments, as well as Aaron’s sons and their garments. (8:30).

And Moses said to Aaron and his sons, “Boil the meat at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting and eat it there with the bread that is in the basket of ordination offerings, as I commanded, saying, ‘Aaron and his sons are to eat it.’ (8:31).
Then you must burn up the remainder of the meat and bread. (8:32).
You must not go outside the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are complete; for it will take seven days to ordain you. (8:33).
What has been done today has been commanded by the LORD in order to make atonement on your behalf. (8:34).
You must remain at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting day and night for seven days and keep the LORD’s charge so that you will not die, for this is what I have been commanded.” (8:35).
So Aaron and his sons did everything the LORD had commanded through Moses. (8:36).
crossRefs: Exodus 29:1-37: The instructions for exactly this seven-day ordination.
Exodus 28:1-43: The garments Moses puts on Aaron piece by piece in this chapter.
Exodus 40:12-15: Moses commanded to wash, clothe, and anoint Aaron and his sons at the tent entrance.
Numbers 3:1-4: Aaron's four sons named, and the two who later died before the LORD.
Hebrews 5:4: No one takes this honor on himself; he is called by God, just as Aaron was.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָשַׁח (mashach), to smear or rub with oil - מָשִׁיחַ (mashiach), an anointed one
translationNotes.note: Oil is poured on Aaron's head at 8:12 and sprinkled on the altar and its utensils at 8:10-11, which puts a person and a set of objects into the same category: taken out of ordinary use. Kings were installed the same way (1 Samuel 16:13; 1 Kings 1:39). The passive form of the verb gives mashiach, which English carries over as Messiah, and the Greek equivalent christos gives Christ.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִלֻּאִים (milluim) - the phrase מִלֵּא יָד (mille yad), 'to fill the hand'
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew for installing a man in an office is to fill his hand, and Leviticus 8:27 acts it out: the fat, the bread and the right thigh are put into Aaron's hands and waved before the LORD. The ram used is called the ram of milluim, the ram of fillings (8:22). The rite ran seven days and the men did not leave the tent entrance for any of them (8:33-35).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה (miḥūts la-maḥaneh), Greek: ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς (exō tēs parembolēs), Aramaic: לבר מן מדברא (lebar men midbara)
translationNotes.note: Place for burning sacrificial remains and carrying out bodies; symbolizes removal of impurity from the holy camp.

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

The ordination ran a full week, with Aaron and his sons confined to the entrance of the tent day and night (8:33-35). The same seven-day pattern governs the consecration of the altar in Exodus 29:37 and the cleansing of a healed skin disease in Leviticus 14:8-9.

Nezer means a consecration or a crown, and it is the same root as nazir, the Nazirite of Numbers 6. The gold plate reading HOLY TO THE LORD was tied over the front of the turban with a blue cord (Exodus 28:36-38). 2 Kings 11:12 uses nezer of the crown put on the boy king Joash.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses consecrates Aaron and his sons as priests by washing them, clothing them in priestly garments, anointing them with oil, and performing sacrifices with a bull, two rams, and bread offerings; Aaron and his sons must remain at the tent of meeting for seven days.

headings.text: Moses Consecrates Aaron and His Sons

stories.title: 🩸 Leviticus 9
summaryBullets: On the eighth day Moses summoned Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel. (9:1).
He said to Aaron, “Take for yourself a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and present them before the LORD. (9:2).
Then speak to the Israelites and say, ‘Take a male goat for a sin offering, a calf and a lamb — both a year old and without blemish — for a burnt offering, (9:3).
an ox and a ram for a peace offering to sacrifice before the LORD, and a grain offering mixed with oil. For today the LORD will appear to you.’” (9:4).
So they took what Moses had commanded to the front of the Tent of Meeting, and the whole congregation drew near and stood before the LORD. (9:5).
And Moses said, “This is what the LORD has commanded you to do, so that the glory of the LORD may appear to you.” (9:6).

Then Moses said to Aaron, “Approach the altar and sacrifice your sin offering and your burnt offering to make atonement for yourself and for the people. And sacrifice the people’s offering to make atonement for them, as the LORD has commanded.” (9:7).
So Aaron approached the altar and slaughtered the calf as a sin offering for himself. (9:8).
The sons of Aaron brought the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and applied it to the horns of the altar. And he poured out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. (9:9).
On the altar he burned the fat, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver from the sin offering, as the LORD had commanded Moses. (9:10).
But he burned up the flesh and the hide outside the camp. (9:11).
Then Aaron slaughtered the burnt offering. His sons brought him the blood, and he splattered it on all sides of the altar. (9:12).
They brought him the burnt offering piece by piece, including the head, and he burned them on the altar. (9:13).
He washed the entrails and the legs and burned them atop the burnt offering on the altar. (9:14).
Aaron then presented the people’s offering. He took the male goat for the people’s sin offering, slaughtered it, and offered it for sin like the first one. (9:15).
He presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the ordinance. (9:16).
Next he presented the grain offering, took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar in addition to the morning’s burnt offering. (9:17).
Then he slaughtered the ox and the ram as the people’s peace offering. His sons brought him the blood, and he splattered it on all sides of the altar. (9:18).
They also brought the fat portions from the ox and the ram— the fat tail, the fat covering the entrails, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver— (9:19).
and placed these on the breasts. Aaron burned the fat portions on the altar, (9:20).
but he waved the breasts and the right thigh as a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses had commanded. (9:21).
Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them. And having made the sin offering, the burnt offering, and the peace offering, he stepped down. (9:22).
Moses and Aaron then entered the Tent of Meeting. When they came out, they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. (9:23).
Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the fat portions on the altar. And when all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown. (9:24).
crossRefs: Leviticus 8:33-35: The seven days of ordination that had to be completed before this eighth day.
Numbers 6:22-27: The words the priests are given to bless Israel with.
Judges 6:21: Fire flares up from the rock and consumes Gideon's offering.
1 Kings 18:38-39: Fire falls from the LORD, consumes the offering, and the people fall facedown.
2 Chronicles 7:1-3: Fire comes down and the glory of the LORD fills the temple at its dedication.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה (miḥūts la-maḥaneh), Greek: ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς (exō tēs parembolēs), Aramaic: לבר מן מדברא (lebar men midbara)
translationNotes.note: Place for burning sacrificial remains and carrying out bodies; symbolizes removal of impurity from the holy camp.

The day after the week of ordination closed, and the first day Aaron served as priest in his own right. The eighth day recurs across the book as the day a completed process is fulfilled: circumcision in Leviticus 12:3, the cleansed man's offerings in 14:10, and the close of Booths in 23:36.

translationNotes.term: lifted up his hands and blessed them
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיִּשָּׂא אַהֲרֹן אֶת־יָדָיו (vayyissa Aharon et-yadav)
translationNotes.note: The first priestly blessing in Scripture, given with raised hands. Numbers 6:22-27 supplies the words. Luke 24:50 shows the same posture at the ascension, hands lifted while blessing.

translationNotes.term: fire came out from the LORD
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַתֵּצֵא אֵשׁ מִלִּפְנֵי יְהוָה (vattetse esh millifne YHWH)
translationNotes.note: At 9:24 the offering on the altar is consumed by fire from God rather than lit by a priest, and the people shout and fall on their faces. The same sentence opens the next chapter with the opposite outcome, when the same fire consumes Nadab and Abihu (10:2). Judges 6:21, 1 Kings 18:38 and 1 Chronicles 21:26 all record fire falling on an offering as the sign that it was accepted.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַטָּאת, עֹלָה, מִנְחָה, שְׁלָמִים (chattat, olah, minchah, shelamim)
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 9 is the first working day of the priesthood and it runs the offerings in a fixed sequence: sin offering first, then burnt offering, then grain offering, then peace offerings (9:8-21). The order matters because it is the one the book keeps: purification first, then whole surrender, then gift, then the shared meal. Aaron offers for himself before he offers for the people (9:7), a rule Hebrews 7:27 points to.

stories.keyTakeaway: Aaron performs the prescribed sacrifices for himself and the people on the eighth day; fire comes from the LORD and consumes the offering, prompting the people to shout and fall facedown.

stories.title: 🩸 Leviticus 10
summaryBullets: Now Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu took their censers, put fire in them and added incense, and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command. (10:1).
So fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them, and they died in the presence of the LORD. (10:2).

Then Moses said to Aaron, “This is what the LORD meant when He said: ‘To those who come near Me I will show My holiness, and in the sight of all the people I will reveal My glory.’” But Aaron remained silent. (10:3).
Moses summoned Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Aaron’s uncle Uzziel, and said to them, “Come here; carry the bodies of your cousins outside the camp, away from the front of the sanctuary.” (10:4).
So they came forward and carried them, still in their tunics, outside the camp, as Moses had directed. (10:5).

Then Moses said to Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar, “Do not let your hair become disheveled and do not tear your garments, or else you will die, and the LORD will be angry with the whole congregation. But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, may mourn on account of the fire that the LORD has ignited. (10:6).
You shall not go outside the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, or you will die, for the LORD’s anointing oil is on you.” So they did as Moses instructed. (10:7).
Then the LORD said to Aaron, (10:8).
“You and your sons are not to drink wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting, or else you will die; this is a permanent statute for the generations to come. (10:9).
You must distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean, (10:10).
so that you may teach the Israelites all the statutes that the LORD has given them through Moses.” (10:11).

And Moses said to Aaron and his remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, “Take the grain offering that remains from the food offerings to the LORD and eat it without leaven beside the altar, because it is most holy. (10:12).
You shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your share and your sons’ share of the food offerings to the LORD; for this is what I have been commanded. (10:13).

And you and your sons and daughters may eat the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution in a ceremonially clean place, because these portions have been assigned to you and your children from the peace offerings of the sons of Israel. (10:14).

They are to bring the thigh of the contribution and the breast of the wave offering, together with the fat portions of the food offerings, to wave as a wave offering before the LORD. It will belong permanently to you and your children, as the LORD has commanded.” (10:15).
Later, Moses searched carefully for the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it had been burned up. He was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s remaining sons, and asked, (10:16).
“Why didn’t you eat the sin offering in the holy place? For it is most holy; it was given to you to take away the guilt of the congregation by making atonement for them before the LORD. (10:17).
Since its blood was not brought inside the holy place, you should have eaten it in the sanctuary area, as I commanded.” (10:18).

But Aaron replied to Moses, “Behold, this very day they presented their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD. Since these things have happened to me, if I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?” (10:19).
And when Moses heard this explanation, he was satisfied. (10:20).
crossRefs: Numbers 3:2-4: Nadab and Abihu die before the LORD and leave no sons.
Numbers 26:61: The second census records again that they died offering unauthorized fire.
Exodus 30:9: The standing prohibition against offering unauthorized incense on the golden altar.
Ezekiel 44:21: No priest is to drink wine before entering the inner court.
Ezekiel 44:23: The priests are to teach the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵשׁ זָרָה (esh zarah), literally 'strange fire'
translationNotes.note: Zar means foreign or belonging to someone else, the same word used of an outsider who may not eat holy food (22:10). The coals for the incense were to be taken from the altar itself (16:12), so fire brought from anywhere else broke the one rule governing the whole procedure. Leviticus 10:1 says plainly that they offered fire He had not commanded them, and 10:9 follows immediately with a ban on priests drinking wine before entering the tent.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה (miḥūts la-maḥaneh), Greek: ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς (exō tēs parembolēs), Aramaic: לבר מן מדברא (lebar men midbara)
translationNotes.note: Place for burning sacrificial remains and carrying out bodies; symbolizes removal of impurity from the holy camp.

Olive oil mixed with specific spices (Exodus 30:22-25), used to consecrate priests, kings, and tabernacle furniture. The Hebrew word for an anointed one is mashiach; transliterated 'Messiah.' The Greek equivalent is christos.

A metal pan for carrying live coals from the altar, with incense laid on top. Numbers 16:6-7 has Korah's company each take one, and Numbers 16:39 has the bronze ones hammered into altar plating afterward. It was a priest's tool, and Nadab and Abihu used theirs with fire the LORD had not commanded.

translationNotes.term: holy and common, clean and unclean
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קֹדֶשׁ / חֹל (qodesh / chol) - טָמֵא / טָהוֹר (tame / tahor)
translationNotes.note: Two separate pairs, not one sliding scale, and Leviticus 10:10 makes teaching the difference part of the priest's job. Holy and common describe what is set apart to God and what is not. Clean and unclean describe ritual status. A thing can be common and clean at the same time, which is the ordinary condition of most of life.

Yayin is grape wine; shekhar covers other fermented drink, including that made from grain or dates. The ban applies to priests on duty in the tent (10:9), and the Nazirite vow in Numbers 6:3 extends it further. Ezekiel 44:21 repeats it for the priests of the restored temple.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD and are consumed by fire from his presence; Moses then establishes rules for Aaron and his remaining sons regarding conduct in the tent of meeting, dietary restrictions, and the eating of holy offerings.

headings.text: The Sin of Nadab and Abihu

stories.title: 🚫 Leviticus 11
summaryBullets: The LORD spoke again to Moses and Aaron, telling them, (11:1).
“Say to the Israelites, ‘Of all the beasts of the earth, these ones you may eat: (11:2).
You may eat any animal that has a split hoof completely divided and that chews the cud. (11:3).
But of those that only chew the cud or only have a divided hoof, you are not to eat the following: The camel, though it chews the cud, does not have a divided hoof; it is unclean for you. (11:4).
The rock badger, though it chews the cud, does not have a divided hoof; it is unclean for you. (11:5).
The rabbit, though it chews the cud, does not have a divided hoof; it is unclean for you. (11:6).
And the pig, though it has a split hoof completely divided, does not chew the cud; it is unclean for you. (11:7).
You must not eat their meat or touch their carcasses; they are unclean for you. (11:8).
Of all the creatures that live in the water, whether in the seas or in the streams, you may eat anything with fins and scales. (11:9).
But the following among all the teeming life and creatures in the water are detestable to you: everything in the seas or streams that does not have fins and scales. (11:10).
They shall be an abomination to you; you must not eat their meat, and you must detest their carcasses. (11:11).
Everything in the water that does not have fins and scales shall be detestable to you. (11:12).
Additionally, you are to detest the following birds, and they must not be eaten because they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, (11:13).
the kite, any kind of falcon, (11:14).
any kind of raven, (11:15).
the ostrich, the screech owl, the gull, any kind of hawk, (11:16).
the little owl, the cormorant, the great owl, (11:17).
the white owl, the desert owl, the osprey, (11:18).
the stork, any kind of heron, the hoopoe, and the bat. (11:19).
All flying insects that walk on all fours are detestable to you. (11:20).
However, you may eat the following kinds of flying insects that walk on all fours: those having jointed legs above their feet for hopping on the ground. (11:21).
Of these you may eat any kind of locust, katydid, cricket, or grasshopper. (11:22).
All other flying insects that have four legs are detestable to you. (11:23).
These creatures will make you unclean. Whoever touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening, (11:24).
and whoever picks up one of their carcasses must wash his clothes, and he will be unclean until evening. (11:25).
Every animal with hooves not completely divided or that does not chew the cud is unclean for you. Whoever touches any of them will be unclean. (11:26).
All the four-footed animals that walk on their paws are unclean for you; whoever touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening, (11:27).
and anyone who picks up a carcass must wash his clothes, and he will be unclean until evening. They are unclean for you. (11:28).
The following creatures that move along the ground are unclean for you: the mole, the mouse, any kind of great lizard, (11:29).
the gecko, the monitor lizard, the common lizard, the skink, and the chameleon. (11:30).
These animals are unclean for you among all the crawling creatures. Whoever touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until evening. (11:31).

When one of them dies and falls on something, that article becomes unclean; any article of wood, clothing, leather, sackcloth, or any implement used for work must be rinsed with water and will remain unclean until evening; then it will be clean. (11:32).
If any of them falls into a clay pot, everything in it will be unclean; you must break the pot. (11:33).
Any food coming into contact with water from that pot will be unclean, and any drink in such a container will be unclean. (11:34).
Anything upon which one of their carcasses falls will be unclean. If it is an oven or cooking pot, it must be smashed; it is unclean and will remain unclean for you. (11:35).
Nevertheless, a spring or cistern containing water will remain clean, but one who touches a carcass in it will be unclean. (11:36).
If a carcass falls on any seed for sowing, the seed is clean; (11:37).
but if water has been put on the seed and a carcass falls on it, it is unclean for you. (11:38).
If an animal that you may eat dies, anyone who touches the carcass will be unclean until evening. (11:39).
Whoever eats from the carcass must wash his clothes and will be unclean until evening, and anyone who picks up the carcass must wash his clothes and will be unclean until evening. (11:40).
Every creature that moves along the ground is detestable; it must not be eaten. (11:41).
Do not eat any creature that moves along the ground, whether it crawls on its belly or walks on four or more feet; for such creatures are detestable. (11:42).
Do not defile yourselves by any crawling creature; do not become unclean or defiled by them. (11:43).
For I am the LORD your God; consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, because I am holy. You must not defile yourselves by any creature that crawls along the ground. (11:44).
For I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt so that I would be your God; therefore be holy, because I am holy. (11:45).
This is the law regarding animals, birds, all living creatures that move in the water, and all creatures that crawl along the ground. (11:46).
You must distinguish between the unclean and the clean, between animals that may be eaten and those that may not.’” (11:47).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 14:3-21: The same list of clean and unclean creatures, with some differences of order and detail.
Genesis 7:2-3: Noah takes clean animals by sevens and unclean by twos, long before Sinai.
Acts 10:9-16: Peter's vision of the sheet, and the voice telling him not to call unclean what God has cleansed.
Ezekiel 4:14: Ezekiel protests that he has never eaten anything unclean in his life.
Daniel 1:8-16: Daniel refuses the king's food and asks for vegetables and water instead.

translationNotes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

These are ritual categories, not verdicts about hygiene, health, or sin. Being unclean is a status that bars a person from the sanctuary until it lapses or is washed off; most cases end at sunset (11:24-25). Ordinary life produced it constantly, and nothing in Leviticus calls an unclean person guilty for being unclean.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַפְרֶסֶת פַּרְסָה וּמַעֲלַת גֵּרָה (mafreset parsah u-maalat gerah)
translationNotes.note: The text gives observable tests, not reasons. A land animal must have a fully split hoof and bring up the cud, and both are required, which is why the camel and the pig each fail on one count (11:4-7). Water creatures need fins and scales (11:9); insects need jointed legs for hopping (11:21).

Leviticus 11 uses sheqets, a word reserved for these creatures and what touches them. The stronger term toevah, usually rendered abomination, is the one used for moral offenses in Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13. English blurs two different Hebrew words into one.

Leviticus 11:13-19 never gives a rule for birds, only a list of about twenty. Nearly all of them are birds of prey, carrion eaters, or waders, and the bat is counted with them. Several of the Hebrew names cannot now be matched to a species with certainty, which is why English versions differ from one another in this list.

Leviticus 11:7 gives the pig its own line because it is the near miss: the hoof is split clean through, but it brings up no cud. Pigs were farmed and eaten all around Israel, and Isaiah 65:4 and 66:17 place the eating of pig flesh inside pagan rites, among the graves and in the sacred groves. Refusing pork became the most visible thing that marked a Jew off from his neighbors in the ancient world.

translationNotes.term: why the clay pot is smashed
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 11:32-36 treats a vessel by what it is made of. Ancient earthenware is porous and cannot be scoured out, so a clay pot or a clay oven that takes uncleanness is broken and thrown away. Wood, cloth, leather, and sackcloth are only rinsed and are clean at sunset, and a spring or a cistern stays clean because running and stored water is not a container. The rule follows the material, not the price of the object.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses and Aaron on which animals the Israelites may eat: land animals with divided hooves that chew cud, water creatures with fins and scales, and certain insects; all others are unclean, and touching their carcasses causes ceremonial uncleanness until evening.

stories.title: 🚫 Leviticus 12
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (12:1).
“Say to the Israelites, ‘A woman who becomes pregnant and gives birth to a son will be unclean for seven days, as she is during the days of her menstruation. (12:2).
And on the eighth day the flesh of the boy’s foreskin is to be circumcised. (12:3).
The woman shall continue in purification from her bleeding for thirty-three days. She must not touch anything sacred or go into the sanctuary until the days of her purification are complete. (12:4).

If, however, she gives birth to a daughter, the woman will be unclean for two weeks as she is during her menstruation. Then she must continue in purification from her bleeding for sixty-six days. (12:5).

When the days of her purification are complete, whether for a son or for a daughter, she is to bring to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering. (12:6).

And the priest will present them before the LORD and make atonement for her; and she shall be ceremonially cleansed from her flow of blood. This is the law for a woman giving birth, whether to a male or to a female. (12:7).

But if she cannot afford a lamb, she shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. Then the priest will make atonement for her, and she will be clean.’” (12:8).
crossRefs: Leviticus 15:19-30: The parallel laws on discharges, closing with the same offering of two birds.
Luke 2:22-24: Mary brings the pair of birds this chapter allows for those who cannot afford a lamb.
Genesis 17:9-12: Circumcision on the eighth day commanded to Abraham and his household.
Luke 1:59: The neighbors come on the eighth day to circumcise John.
Leviticus 20:18: The prohibition tied to a woman's flow of blood.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁלֹשִׁים וּשְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים (sheloshim u-sheloshet yamim), 'thirty-three days'
translationNotes.note: Seven days of uncleanness plus thirty-three of purification for a son, doubled to fourteen plus sixty-six for a daughter (12:2-5). The text gives the counts without giving a reason for the difference. Luke 2:22 places the presentation of Jesus at the end of the first of these periods.

The prescribed offering is a year-old lamb plus a bird, and Leviticus 12:8 allows two birds instead if a lamb is out of reach. Luke 2:24 records exactly the second option being brought for Jesus, which places His family among those the concession was written for.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יִמּוֹל בְּשַׂר עָרְלָתוֹ (yimmol besar orlato)
translationNotes.note: The one command inside a chapter otherwise about the mother, set at 12:3 on the eighth day after birth. It goes back to Genesis 17:10-12, where the same eighth day is fixed for Abraham's household. Luke 1:59 and 2:21 both record it being kept on schedule, and Philippians 3:5 has Paul citing his own on the eighth day as a credential.

translationNotes.term: she must not touch anything sacred
translationNotes.note: The restriction at 12:4 is about access to the sanctuary and its food, not about the household. Thirty-three days for a son and sixty-six for a daughter follow the initial period, and only when they are complete does she bring the offering at 12:6. Luke 2:22-24 records Mary bringing the two birds of 12:8, which the law allows when a lamb is beyond the family's means.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD establishes purification periods for women after childbirth: seven days plus thirty-three days for a son, fourteen days plus sixty-six days for a daughter; after this time, they bring a lamb and a bird to the priest for atonement, or two birds if they cannot afford a lamb.

stories.title: 🚫 Leviticus 13
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, (13:1).
“When someone has a swelling or rash or bright spot on his skin that may be an infectious skin disease, he must be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons who is a priest. (13:2).

The priest is to examine the infection on his skin, and if the hair in the infection has turned white and the sore appears to be deeper than the skin, it is a skin disease. After the priest examines him, he must pronounce him unclean. (13:3).

If, however, the spot on his skin is white and does not appear to be deeper than the skin, and the hair in it has not turned white, the priest shall isolate the infected person for seven days. (13:4).
On the seventh day the priest is to reexamine him, and if he sees that the infection is unchanged and has not spread on the skin, the priest must isolate him for another seven days. (13:5).

The priest will examine him again on the seventh day, and if the sore has faded and has not spread on the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is a rash. The person must wash his clothes and be clean. (13:6).
But if the rash spreads further on his skin after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he must present himself again to the priest. (13:7).
The priest will reexamine him, and if the rash has spread on the skin, the priest must pronounce him unclean; it is a skin disease. (13:8).
When anyone develops a skin disease, he must be brought to the priest. (13:9).
The priest will examine him, and if there is a white swelling on the skin that has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling, (13:10).
it is a chronic skin disease and the priest must pronounce him unclean. He need not isolate him, for he is unclean. (13:11).
But if the skin disease breaks out all over his skin so that it covers all the skin of the infected person from head to foot, as far as the priest can see, (13:12).
the priest shall examine him, and if the disease has covered his entire body, he is to pronounce the infected person clean. Since it has all turned white, he is clean. (13:13).
But whenever raw flesh appears on someone, he will be unclean. (13:14).
When the priest sees the raw flesh, he must pronounce him unclean. The raw flesh is unclean; it is a skin disease. (13:15).
But if the raw flesh changes and turns white, he must go to the priest. (13:16).
The priest will reexamine him, and if the infection has turned white, the priest is to pronounce the infected person clean; then he is clean. (13:17).
When a boil appears on someone’s skin and it heals, (13:18).
and a white swelling or a reddish-white spot develops where the boil was, he must present himself to the priest. (13:19).
