If anyone eats a sacred offering in error, he must add a fifth to its value and give the sacred offering to the priest. (22:14).
The priests must not profane the sacred offerings that the Israelites present to the LORD (22:15).
by allowing the people to eat the sacred offerings and thus to bear the punishment for guilt. For I am the LORD who sanctifies them.” (22:16).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (22:17).

“Speak to Aaron and his sons and all the Israelites and tell them, ‘Any man of the house of Israel or any foreign resident who presents a gift for a burnt offering to the LORD, whether to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering, (22:18).
must offer an unblemished male from the cattle, sheep, or goats in order for it to be accepted on your behalf. (22:19).
You must not present anything with a defect, because it will not be accepted on your behalf. (22:20).
When a man presents a peace offering to the LORD from the herd or flock to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering, it must be without blemish or defect to be acceptable. (22:21).

You are not to present to the LORD any animal that is blind, injured, or maimed, or anything with a running sore, a festering rash, or a scab; you must not put any of these on the altar as a food offering to the LORD. (22:22).
You may present as a freewill offering an ox or sheep that has a deformed or stunted limb, but it is not acceptable in fulfillment of a vow. (22:23).
You are not to present to the LORD an animal whose testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut; you are not to sacrifice them in your land. (22:24).
Neither you nor a foreigner shall present food to your God from any such animal. They will not be accepted on your behalf, because they are deformed and flawed.’” (22:25).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (22:26).
“When an ox, a sheep, or a goat is born, it must remain with its mother for seven days. From the eighth day on, it will be acceptable as a food offering presented to the LORD. (22:27).
But you must not slaughter an ox or a sheep on the same day as its young. (22:28).
When you sacrifice a thank offering to the LORD, offer it so that it may be acceptable on your behalf. (22:29).
It must be eaten that same day. Do not leave any of it until morning. I am the LORD. (22:30).
You are to keep My commandments and practice them. I am the LORD. (22:31).
You must not profane My holy name. I must be acknowledged as holy among the Israelites. I am the LORD who sanctifies you, (22:32).
who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. I am the LORD.” (22:33).
crossRefs: Malachi 1:6-14: Priests rebuked for bringing blind, lame, and diseased animals to the altar.
Deuteronomy 15:21: An animal with any serious defect is not to be sacrificed to the LORD.
Leviticus 21:16-23: The matching requirement that the priest himself be without defect.
Numbers 18:8-13: The holy offerings assigned to the priests and their households as their food.
1 Peter 1:19: The precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָלַל (ḥālal), Greek: βεβηλόω (bebēloō), Aramaic: חלל (ḥll)
translationNotes.note: To treat something holy as common or ordinary.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוּם (mum), a defect - תָּמִים (tamim), whole or sound
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 22:20-25 lists what rules an animal out of an offering: blind, injured, maimed, with a wart, a festering sore or a running sore, and anything with bruised, crushed, torn or cut parts. The same word bars a priest from serving at the altar in 21:17-23, though 21:22 lets him eat the holy food. Malachi 1:8 charges Israel with breaking exactly this rule by bringing the blind and lame animals to the altar.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָדַשׁ (qadash), Greek: ἁγιάζω (hagiazō), Aramaic: קדש (qdsh)
translationNotes.note: To set apart as holy; God sanctifies priests and offerings.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וּבָא הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְטָהֵר (u-va ha-shemesh ve-taher)
translationNotes.note: A priest made unclean bathes and waits for sundown, and then may eat the holy food again (22:6-7). The Hebrew day begins at evening, so sunset both ends the uncleanness and starts the new day. This is the rhythm behind Mark 1:32, where the crowds come to Jesus after sunset on the Sabbath.

A neder is a promise already made and now owed; a nedavah is given with no obligation behind it. Leviticus 22:23 lets a slightly deformed animal serve as a freewill offering but not in payment of a vow, because a vow names what will be brought. Deuteronomy 23:21-23 warns against making one lightly.

translationNotes.term: not on the same day as its young
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 22:28 forbids slaughtering a parent animal and its offspring on one day, and 22:27 requires a newborn to stay with its mother seven days first. Deuteronomy 22:6-7 gives the matching rule for a bird's nest, releasing the mother before taking the young.

stories.keyTakeaway: Moses is told to instruct Aaron and his sons that priests must be ceremonially clean to eat sacred offerings, and that only certain family members may consume them. God also specifies that all animals presented as offerings must be without defect, and gives rules about timing for young animals and thank offerings.

stories.title: 📅 Leviticus 23
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (23:1).
“Speak to the Israelites and say to them, ‘These are My appointed feasts, the feasts of the LORD that you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies. (23:2).
For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, a day of sacred assembly. You must not do any work; wherever you live, it is a Sabbath to the LORD. (23:3).
These are the LORD’s appointed feasts, the sacred assemblies you are to proclaim at their appointed times. (23:4).
The Passover to the LORD begins at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month. (23:5).
On the fifteenth day of the same month begins the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the LORD. For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. (23:6).
On the first day you are to hold a sacred assembly; you are not to do any regular work. (23:7).
For seven days you are to present a food offering to the LORD. On the seventh day there shall be a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work.’” (23:8).
And the LORD said to Moses, (23:9).
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘When you enter the land that I am giving you and you reap its harvest, you are to bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest. (23:10).
And he shall wave the sheaf before the LORD so that it may be accepted on your behalf; the priest is to wave it on the day after the Sabbath. (23:11).
On the day you wave the sheaf, you shall offer a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering to the LORD, (23:12).
along with its grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil — a food offering to the LORD, a pleasing aroma — and its drink offering of a quarter hin of wine. (23:13).

You must not eat any bread or roasted or new grain until the very day you have brought this offering to your God. This is to be a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live. (23:14).
From the day after the Sabbath, the day you brought the sheaf of the wave offering, you are to count off seven full weeks. (23:15).
You shall count off fifty days until the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the LORD. (23:16).
Bring two loaves of bread from your dwellings as a wave offering, each made from two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour, baked with leaven, as the firstfruits to the LORD. (23:17).

Along with the bread you are to present seven unblemished male lambs a year old, one young bull, and two rams. They will be a burnt offering to the LORD, together with their grain offerings and drink offerings — a food offering, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. (23:18).
You shall also prepare one male goat as a sin offering and two male lambs a year old as a peace offering. (23:19).
The priest is to wave the lambs as a wave offering before the LORD, together with the bread of the firstfruits. The bread and the two lambs shall be holy to the LORD for the priest. (23:20).
On that same day you are to proclaim a sacred assembly, and you must not do any regular work. This is to be a permanent statute wherever you live for the generations to come. (23:21).

When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap all the way to the edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. Leave them for the poor and the foreign resident. I am the LORD your God.’” (23:22).
The LORD also said to Moses, (23:23).
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘On the first day of the seventh month you are to have a day of rest, a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts. (23:24).
You must not do any regular work, but you are to present a food offering to the LORD.’” (23:25).
Again the LORD said to Moses, (23:26).
“The tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. You shall hold a sacred assembly and humble yourselves, and present a food offering to the LORD. (23:27).
On this day you are not to do any work, for it is the Day of Atonement, when atonement is made for you before the LORD your God. (23:28).
If anyone does not humble himself on this day, he must be cut off from his people. (23:29).
I will destroy from among his people anyone who does any work on this day. (23:30).
You are not to do any work at all. This is a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live. (23:31).
It will be a Sabbath of complete rest for you, and you shall humble yourselves. From the evening of the ninth day of the month until the following evening you are to keep your Sabbath.” (23:32).
And the LORD said to Moses, (23:33).
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘On the fifteenth day of the seventh month the Feast of Tabernacles to the LORD begins, and it continues for seven days. (23:34).
On the first day there shall be a sacred assembly. You must not do any regular work. (23:35).

For seven days you are to present a food offering to the LORD. On the eighth day you are to hold a sacred assembly and present a food offering to the LORD. It is a solemn assembly; you must not do any regular work. (23:36).

These are the LORD’s appointed feasts, which you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies for presenting food offerings to the LORD — burnt offerings and grain offerings, sacrifices and drink offerings, each on its designated day. (23:37).
These offerings are in addition to the offerings for the LORD’s Sabbaths, and in addition to your gifts, to all your vow offerings, and to all the freewill offerings you give to the LORD. (23:38).

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, after you have gathered the produce of the land, you are to celebrate a feast to the LORD for seven days. There shall be complete rest on the first day and also on the eighth day. (23:39).

On the first day you are to gather the fruit of majestic trees, the branches of palm trees, and the boughs of leafy trees and of willows of the brook. And you are to rejoice before the LORD your God for seven days. (23:40).
You are to celebrate this as a feast to the LORD for seven days each year. This is a permanent statute for the generations to come; you are to celebrate it in the seventh month. (23:41).
You are to dwell in booths for seven days. All the native-born of Israel must dwell in booths, (23:42).
so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.’” (23:43).
So Moses announced to the Israelites the appointed feasts of the LORD. (23:44).
crossRefs: Exodus 23:14-17: The three pilgrimage feasts first commanded, with no one to appear empty-handed.
Numbers 28:16-29:40: The full sacrificial schedule prescribed for each of these appointed times.
Deuteronomy 16:1-17: Passover, Weeks, and Booths kept at the place the LORD chooses.
Nehemiah 8:13-18: Israel keeps the Feast of Booths in shelters, something not done since the days of Joshua.
Acts 2:1-4: The Spirit is given on the day of Pentecost, the fiftieth day counted from the wave sheaf.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹעֵד (moed), an appointed time or meeting - plural מוֹעֲדִים (moadim)
translationNotes.note: A moed is a fixed appointment, not a holiday. Genesis 1:14 uses the word of what the lights in the sky were made for, and the tent where God met Moses is the ohel moed, the tent of appointment (Exodus 33:7). Leviticus 23:2 calls the list that follows the moadim of the LORD, which puts the dates on His calendar rather than on Israel's, and 23:4 repeats it before naming them one by one.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֻכּוֹת (sukkot), shelters made of branches
translationNotes.note: A sukkah is a rough temporary shelter, the kind thrown up in a field at harvest, and Leviticus 23:42-43 orders Israel to live in them for seven days so that every generation would know that God made their fathers live in shelters when He brought them out of Egypt. The feast falls on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and runs eight days with the closing assembly (23:34-36). Nehemiah 8:14-17 records the practice being taken up again after the exile, and John 7:2 places Jesus in Jerusalem for it.
The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).
The standard temple liquid measure for wine and oil in offerings; about one gallon (3.8 liters). Used throughout Exodus and Numbers for prescribed drink offerings.

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

The first portion of each harvest offered to God before the rest could be eaten (Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 23:9-14). Paul calls the resurrected Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20); the guarantee that the full resurrection harvest will follow.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹעֲדֵי יְהוָה (moade YHWH), 'the appointed times of the LORD'
translationNotes.note: Moed means a fixed appointment, the same word used for the Tent of Meeting in Exodus 27:21. Leviticus 23 lists them by month and day: Passover on the fourteenth of the first month, Unleavened Bread, the wave sheaf, Weeks, the day of trumpet blasts, Atonement, and Booths. Genesis 1:14 uses the same word for what the lights in the sky are set to mark.

The word rendered 'sheaf' here is omer, the same word that names the dry measure of about 2.2 liters in Exodus 16:36. Leviticus 23:15-16 starts a fifty-day count from the day it is waved, which is why that count is still called the counting of the Omer.

The starting point of the fifty-day count to the Feast of Weeks (23:11, 23:15-16). Josephus, writing in Antiquities of the Jews 3.250, records the sheaf being brought on the sixteenth of the month, the second day of Unleavened Bread.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲמִשִּׁים יוֹם (chamishim yom) - Greek: πεντηκοστή (pentekoste), 'fiftieth'
translationNotes.note: Seven full weeks plus one day, which is why the feast is called Weeks in Hebrew and Pentecost in Greek. Its offering is two loaves baked with leaven (23:17), the only leavened bread commanded to the altar. Acts 2:1 places the giving of the Spirit on this day.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זִכְרוֹן תְּרוּעָה (zikhron teruah), 'a memorial of blast'
translationNotes.note: The first day of the seventh month, marked by teruah, the sharp blast or shout also used as a battle signal in Numbers 10:5-6. Numbers 29:1 calls it a day of blowing the horns. Leviticus gives it no other name and states no reason for it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פְּרִי עֵץ הָדָר, כַּפֹּת תְּמָרִים, עֲנַף עֵץ־עָבֹת, עַרְבֵי־נָחַל
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 23:40 names fruit of majestic trees, palm fronds, boughs of leafy trees, and willows of the brook, to be gathered on the first day of Booths. Nehemiah 8:15 sends people to the hills for olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy branches to build the shelters.

translationNotes.term: the calendar these dates sit on
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֹדֶשׁ (chodesh), month, from the word for new
translationNotes.note: Every date in Leviticus 23 counts from a new moon, because the Hebrew month begins when the crescent is first visible and runs 29 or 30 days. The Hebrew word for month is built on the root for new. The first month, called Aviv in Exodus 13:4, falls in March or April, so Passover on the fourteenth lands near the spring equinox and the barley harvest. The seventh month, holding the trumpet blast, the Day of Atonement, and Booths, falls in September or October at the end of the fruit and olive season.

stories.keyTakeaway: God establishes the appointed festivals Israel must observe: Passover and Unleavened Bread in the first month, a wave offering of firstfruits seven weeks later, a day of rest with trumpet blasts on the first day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement on the tenth day of that month, and the Festival of Tabernacles beginning on the fifteenth day. Moses announces these festivals to the Israelites.

headings.text: Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread

stories.title: 📅 Leviticus 24
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (24:1).
“Command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually. (24:2).

Outside the veil of the Testimony in the Tent of Meeting, Aaron is to tend the lamps continually before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the generations to come. (24:3).
He shall tend the lamps on the pure gold lampstand before the LORD continually. (24:4).
You are also to take fine flour and bake twelve loaves, using two-tenths of an ephah for each loaf, (24:5).
and set them in two rows — six per row — on the table of pure gold before the LORD. (24:6).
And you are to place pure frankincense near each row, so that it may serve as a memorial portion for the bread, a food offering to the LORD. (24:7).
Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant. (24:8).
It belongs to Aaron and his sons, who are to eat it in a holy place; for it is to him a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD — his portion forever.” (24:9).
Now the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father went out among the Israelites, and a fight broke out in the camp between him and an Israelite. (24:10).
The son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name with a curse. So they brought him to Moses. (His mother’s name was Shelomith daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.) (24:11).
They placed him in custody until the will of the LORD should be made clear to them. (24:12).
Then the LORD said to Moses, (24:13).
“Take the blasphemer outside the camp, and have all who heard him lay their hands on his head; then have the whole assembly stone him. (24:14).
And you are to tell the Israelites, ‘If anyone curses his God, he shall bear the consequences of his sin. (24:15).

Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD must surely be put to death; the whole assembly must surely stone him, whether he is a foreign resident or native; if he blasphemes the Name, he must be put to death. (24:16).
And if a man takes the life of anyone else, he must surely be put to death. (24:17).
Whoever kills an animal must make restitution — life for life. (24:18).
If anyone injures his neighbor, whatever he has done must be done to him: (24:19).
fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. Just as he injured the other person, the same must be inflicted on him. (24:20).
Whoever kills an animal must make restitution, but whoever kills a man must be put to death. (24:21).
You are to have the same standard of law for the foreign resident and the native; for I am the LORD your God.’” (24:22).
Then Moses spoke to the Israelites, and they took the blasphemer outside the camp and stoned him. So the Israelites did as the LORD had commanded Moses. (24:23).
crossRefs: Exodus 25:23-30: The gold table on which the Bread of the Presence is set out, the arrangement this chapter orders renewed every Sabbath.
Matthew 12:3-4: Jesus cites David eating the consecrated bread that only the priests were allowed to eat, which is the restriction laid down at 24:9.

Deuteronomy 19:17-18: The same eye-for-eye standard is given inside a courtroom, with both parties before the priests and the judges and the judges investigating thoroughly before any sentence; here it is given while the accused sits in custody at 24:12 waiting for a verdict.
Leviticus 19:18: Five chapters earlier the same law forbids revenge and grudge-bearing outright, so the injury sentence at 24:19-20 belongs to the assembly and not to the man who was hurt.
Romans 12:19: Paul quotes 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay' from Deuteronomy 32:35 and tells believers never to avenge themselves.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹעֵד (moʿed), Greek: καιρός (kairos), Aramaic: מועדא (moʿeda)
translationNotes.note: Fixed times or seasons set by God for sacred gatherings.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֻכּוֹת (sukkot), Greek: σκηναί (skēnai), Aramaic: סכתא (sukkta)
translationNotes.note: Temporary shelters made with branches to recall Israel’s wilderness dwelling.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יֹבֵל (yōvel), Greek: ἄφεσις (aphesis, 'release'), Aramaic: יובלא (yovla)
translationNotes.note: The fiftieth year when land reverts, debts are canceled, and slaves are freed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּאֵל (goʾel), Greek: λυτρωτής (lytrōtēs), Aramaic: גלא (gala)
translationNotes.note: A family protector who buys back land or frees relatives from slavery.

About two thirds of a mile (1 km); the rabbinic limit on travel from one's dwelling on the Sabbath, derived from the camp boundaries in Exodus 16:29 and Numbers 35:5. Acts 1:12 places the Mount of Olives this distance from Jerusalem.
translationNotes.original: Greek: σαββάτου ἔχον ὁδόν (sabbatou echon hodon)

translationNotes.note: The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

A milky-white resin from the Boswellia tree of southern Arabia. Burned as incense in the temple (Exodus 30:34); offered with every grain offering. The magi's second gift, traditionally read as signaling priesthood.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים (lechem ha-panim), 'bread of the face'
translationNotes.note: Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, each made from two tenths of an ephah of fine flour, about 4.4 liters apiece, so roughly 53 liters of flour in a single setting. They stood in two rows of six with frankincense beside each row, were replaced every Sabbath, and were then eaten by the priests (24:5-9).

The verb naqav means to pierce or to pronounce distinctly, and the text does not write the name that was used. Leviticus 24:16 makes the offense capital for native and foreigner alike. This passage is the basis for the later Jewish practice of saying 'the Name' in place of pronouncing it.

Leviticus 24:22 states it flatly: the same law for the foreign resident and the native. The case that prompts it involves the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father (24:10). Numbers 15:15-16 and Exodus 12:49 repeat the same principle.

translationNotes.term: Eye for eye as a ceiling
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַיִן תַּחַת עַיִן (ayin tachat ayin), 'an eye in place of an eye' - מוּם (mum), an injury or blemish
translationNotes.note: The formula sets a maximum, not a minimum and not a licence. Leviticus 24:19-20 states the rule twice in plain words around the famous pairs: 'as he has done, so shall it be done to him,' and 'as he has injured a man, so shall it be given to him.' The measure of the penalty is the injury itself, which rules out a family answering a lost tooth with a killing. The same formula appears in Babylon graded by rank, where the laws of Hammurabi take an eye for an eye between men of standing (law 196) but settle a freed man's eye for a mina of silver (198) and a slave's for half his price (199); Leviticus 24:22 answers that with one standard for the foreigner and the native alike.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses on maintaining the lampstand with oil and setting out twelve loaves of bread in the sanctuary as perpetual offerings. When a man of mixed Israelite and Egyptian descent blasphemes God's name, Moses brings the case before the LORD, who commands that the blasphemer be stoned and establishes laws requiring death for blasphemy, life for life in cases of killing, and equivalent injury for assault.

stories.title: 📅 Leviticus 25
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses on Mount Sinai, (25:1).
“Speak to the Israelites and say to them: When you enter the land that I am giving you, the land itself must observe a Sabbath to the LORD. (25:2).
For six years you may sow your field and prune your vineyard and gather its crops. (25:3).
But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of complete rest for the land — a Sabbath to the LORD. You are not to sow your field or prune your vineyard. (25:4).
You are not to reap the aftergrowth of your harvest or gather the grapes of your untended vines. The land must have a year of complete rest. (25:5).
Whatever the land yields during the Sabbath year shall be food for you— for yourself, your manservant and maidservant, the hired hand or foreigner who stays with you, (25:6).
and for your livestock and the wild animals in your land. All its growth may serve as food. (25:7).
And you shall count off seven Sabbaths of years — seven times seven years — so that the seven Sabbaths of years amount to forty-nine years. (25:8).
Then you are to sound the horn far and wide on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement. You shall sound it throughout your land. (25:9).
So you are to consecrate the fiftieth year and proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants. It shall be your Jubilee, when each of you is to return to his property and to his clan. (25:10).
The fiftieth year will be a Jubilee for you; you are not to sow the land or reap its aftergrowth or harvest the untended vines. (25:11).
For it is a Jubilee; it shall be holy to you. You may eat only the crops taken directly from the field. (25:12).
In this Year of Jubilee, each of you shall return to his own property. (25:13).
If you make a sale to your neighbor or a purchase from him, you must not take advantage of each other. (25:14).
You are to buy from your neighbor according to the number of years since the last Jubilee; he is to sell to you according to the number of harvest years remaining. (25:15).
You shall increase the price in proportion to a greater number of years, or decrease it in proportion to a lesser number of years; for he is selling you a given number of harvests. (25:16).
Do not take advantage of each other, but fear your God; for I am the LORD your God. (25:17).
You are to keep My statutes and carefully observe My judgments, so that you may dwell securely in the land. (25:18).
Then the land will yield its fruit, so that you can eat your fill and dwell in safety in the land. (25:19).
Now you may wonder, ‘What will we eat in the seventh year if we do not sow or gather our produce?’ (25:20).
But I will send My blessing upon you in the sixth year, so that the land will yield a crop sufficient for three years. (25:21).
While you are sowing in the eighth year, you will be eating from the previous harvest, until the ninth year’s harvest comes in. (25:22).
The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me. (25:23).
Thus for every piece of property you possess, you must provide for the redemption of the land. (25:24).
If your brother becomes impoverished and sells some of his property, his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold. (25:25).
Or if a man has no one to redeem it for him, but he prospers and acquires enough to redeem his land, (25:26).
he shall calculate the years since its sale, repay the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and return to his property. (25:27).

But if he cannot obtain enough to repay him, what he sold will remain in possession of the buyer until the Year of Jubilee. In the Jubilee, however, it is to be released, so that he may return to his property. (25:28).
If a man sells a house in a walled city, he retains his right of redemption until a full year after its sale; during that year it may be redeemed. (25:29).
If it is not redeemed by the end of a full year, then the house in the walled city is permanently transferred to its buyer and his descendants. It is not to be released in the Jubilee. (25:30).
But houses in villages with no walls around them are to be considered as open fields. They may be redeemed, and they shall be released in the Jubilee. (25:31).
As for the cities of the Levites, the Levites always have the right to redeem their houses in the cities they possess. (25:32).

So whatever belongs to the Levites may be redeemed— a house sold in a city they possess— and must be released in the Jubilee, because the houses in the cities of the Levites are their possession among the Israelites. (25:33).
But the open pastureland around their cities may not be sold, for this is their permanent possession. (25:34).
Now if your countryman becomes destitute and cannot support himself among you, then you are to help him as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you. (25:35).
Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God, that your countryman may live among you. (25:36).
You must not lend him your silver at interest or sell him your food for profit. (25:37).
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to give you the land of Canaan and to be your God. (25:38).
If a countryman among you becomes destitute and sells himself to you, then you must not force him into slave labor. (25:39).
Let him stay with you as a hired worker or temporary resident; he is to work for you until the Year of Jubilee. (25:40).
Then he and his children are to be released, and he may return to his clan and to the property of his fathers. (25:41).
Because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt, they are not to be sold as slaves. (25:42).
You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God. (25:43).
Your menservants and maidservants shall come from the nations around you, from whom you may purchase them. (25:44).
You may also purchase them from the foreigners residing among you or their clans living among you who are born in your land. These may become your property. (25:45).
You may leave them to your sons after you to inherit as property; you can make them slaves for life. But as for your brothers, the Israelites, no man may rule harshly over his brother. (25:46).
If a foreigner residing among you prospers, but your countryman dwelling near him becomes destitute and sells himself to the foreigner or to a member of his clan, (25:47).
he retains the right of redemption after he has sold himself. One of his brothers may redeem him: (25:48).
either his uncle or cousin or any close relative from his clan may redeem him. Or if he prospers, he may redeem himself. (25:49).

He and his purchaser will then count the time from the year he sold himself up to the Year of Jubilee. The price of his sale will be determined by the number of years, based on the daily wages of a hired hand. (25:50).
If many years remain, he must pay for his redemption in proportion to his purchase price. (25:51).
If only a few years remain until the Year of Jubilee, he is to calculate and pay his redemption according to his remaining years. (25:52).
He shall be treated like a man hired from year to year, but a foreign owner must not rule over him harshly in your sight. (25:53).
Even if he is not redeemed in any of these ways, he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee. (25:54).
For the Israelites are My servants. They are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God. (25:55).
crossRefs: Exodus 23:10-11: The seventh-year rest for the land, first commanded at Sinai.
2 Chronicles 36:20-21: The exile runs until the land has enjoyed the sabbaths it was owed.
Ruth 4:1-10: Boaz acts as kinsman-redeemer and buys back the field along with the widow.
Jeremiah 32:6-12: Jeremiah buys his cousin's field at Anathoth because the right of redemption is his.
Isaiah 61:1-2: Good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, and the year of the LORD's favor.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מוֹעֵד (moʿed), Greek: καιρός (kairos), Aramaic: מועדא (moʿeda)
translationNotes.note: Fixed times or seasons set by God for sacred gatherings.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֻכּוֹת (sukkot), Greek: σκηναί (skēnai), Aramaic: סכתא (sukkta)
translationNotes.note: Temporary shelters made with branches to recall Israel’s wilderness dwelling.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּאֵל (goʾel), Greek: λυτρωτής (lytrōtēs), Aramaic: גלא (gala)
translationNotes.note: A family protector who buys back land or frees relatives from slavery.

The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.

Every 50th year, after seven sabbatical-year cycles (Leviticus 25). Land returned to original families, Hebrew slaves were freed, and debts cancelled; a structural reset of social and economic inequality. The 'year of the Lord's favor' Jesus proclaims in Luke 4:19 draws directly on jubilee language from Isaiah 61.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁנַת שַׁבָּתוֹן (shenat shabbaton), later שְׁמִטָּה (shemittah), 'release'
translationNotes.note: Every seventh year no sowing, no pruning, no organized harvest; whatever grows on its own is open to the owner, his servants, hired hands, resident foreigners, livestock, and wild animals alike (25:5-7). Leviticus 25:20-22 answers the obvious objection with a promised triple crop in the sixth year. 2 Chronicles 36:21 counts the exile as the land collecting what it was owed.

The name is the instrument: the horn sounded on the Day of Atonement of the forty-ninth year to open the fiftieth (25:9-10). Land returned to the family that first held it and Israelite debt-servants went home. The Greek Old Testament renders it aphesis, release, the same word behind forgiveness in the New Testament.

Deror means release from bondage or debt, and Jeremiah 34:8-17 records a proclamation of it in Jerusalem that was made and then revoked. The King James rendering of Leviticus 25:10 is the inscription cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia in 1751.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא תִמָּכֵר לִצְמִתֻת (lo timmakher litsmitut), 'not sold permanently'
translationNotes.note: Nobody in Israel could sell land outright. What changed hands was the number of harvests left before the next Jubilee, and the price rose or fell with that count (25:15-16). Leviticus 25:23 gives the reason: the land is the LORD's, and Israel holds it as resident tenants.

A house inside a walled town could be redeemed for one year and then passed permanently to the buyer; a house in an unwalled village counted as open country and returned at the Jubilee (25:29-31). Levite houses were exempt from the rule and always redeemable (25:32-33).

Two words for two forms of the same thing: interest deducted at the front and profit added at the back. Leviticus 25:36-37 bans both toward an impoverished Israelite, on money and on food. Ezekiel 18:8 and 22:12 use the pair as a test of a righteous man.

Leviticus 25:43 and 25:46 both forbid ruling over an Israelite be-farekh, and the word is not a general term for strictness. It appears at Exodus 1:13-14, twice, for what Egypt did to Israel: they made them serve be-farekh and made their lives bitter with hard labor. The law reaches for the reader's own memory of slavery and forbids reproducing it. Verse 25:39 says the same thing from the other side: you shall not make him serve as a slave serves.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּי־עֲבָדַי הֵם (ki avadai hem), 'for they are My servants'
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 25:42 and 25:55 give the stated ground for every limit in the chapter: the Israelites are God's servants, whom He brought out of Egypt, and so they are not to be sold as slaves are sold. The claim is one of prior ownership, which is why the jubilee can cancel a sale and send a man home. Verse 25:23 applies the same logic to the ground itself, saying the land is not to be sold permanently because the land is His and Israel are resident foreigners on it.

translationNotes.term: The right to be bought back
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גְּאֻלָּה (geullah), redemption - גֹּאֵל (goel), the kinsman-redeemer
translationNotes.note: Leviticus 25:47-55 covers an Israelite who has sold himself to a resident foreigner, and the sale never becomes final. He keeps the right of redemption after it, and the list of who may exercise it is wide: a brother, an uncle, an uncle's son, any blood relative, or the man himself if he prospers (25:48-49). The price is calculated by the harvests remaining until the jubilee, so it falls each year (25:50-52). Verse 53 adds that the buyer must not rule over him with rigor in the sight of Israel. The same office of goel buys back family land at 25:25 and stands behind Boaz in Ruth 4.

stories.keyTakeaway: God commands Israel to observe every seventh year as a rest year for the land, and every fiftieth year as a jubilee when all land returns to original owners and fellow Israelites are released from servitude; rules are given for land sales, redemption of property, treatment of the poor, and distinctions between Hebrew servants and foreign slaves.

stories.title: ⚖️ Leviticus 26
summaryBullets: “You must not make idols for yourselves or set up a carved image or sacred pillar; you must not place a sculpted stone in your land to bow down to it. For I am the LORD your God. (26:1).
You must keep My Sabbaths and have reverence for My sanctuary. I am the LORD. (26:2).
If you follow My statutes and carefully keep My commandments, (26:3).
I will give you rains in their season, and the land will yield its produce, and the trees of the field will bear their fruit. (26:4).
Your threshing will continue until the grape harvest, and the grape harvest will continue until sowing time; you will have your fill of food to eat and will dwell securely in your land. (26:5).
And I will give peace to the land, and you will lie down with nothing to fear. I will rid the land of dangerous animals, and no sword will pass through your land. (26:6).
You will pursue your enemies, and they will fall by the sword before you. (26:7).
Five of you will pursue a hundred, and a hundred of you will pursue ten thousand, and your enemies will fall by the sword before you. (26:8).
I will turn toward you and make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will establish My covenant with you. (26:9).
You will still be eating the old supply of grain when you need to clear it out to make room for the new. (26:10).
And I will make My dwelling place among you, and My soul will not despise you. (26:11).
I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people. (26:12).
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt so that you would no longer be slaves to the Egyptians. I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk in uprightness. (26:13).
If, however, you fail to obey Me and to carry out all these commandments, (26:14).
and if you reject My statutes, despise My ordinances, and neglect to carry out all My commandments, and so break My covenant, (26:15).

then this is what I will do to you: I will bring upon you sudden terror, wasting disease, and fever that will destroy your sight and drain your life. You will sow your seed in vain, because your enemies will eat it. (26:16).
And I will set My face against you, so that you will be defeated by your enemies. Those who hate you will rule over you, and you will flee when no one pursues you. (26:17).
And if after all this you will not obey Me, I will proceed to punish you sevenfold for your sins. (26:18).
I will break down your stubborn pride and make your sky like iron and your land like bronze, (26:19).
and your strength will be spent in vain. For your land will not yield its produce, and the trees of the land will not bear their fruit. (26:20).
If you walk in hostility toward Me and refuse to obey Me, I will multiply your plagues seven times, according to your sins. (26:21).
I will send wild animals against you to rob you of your children, destroy your livestock, and reduce your numbers, until your roads lie desolate. (26:22).
And if in spite of these things you do not accept My discipline, but continue to walk in hostility toward Me, (26:23).
then I will act with hostility toward you, and I will strike you sevenfold for your sins. (26:24).

And I will bring a sword against you to execute the vengeance of the covenant. Though you withdraw into your cities, I will send a plague among you, and you will be delivered into the hand of the enemy. (26:25).
When I cut off your supply of bread, ten women will bake your bread in a single oven and dole out your bread by weight, so that you will eat but not be satisfied. (26:26).
But if in spite of all this you do not obey Me, but continue to walk in hostility toward Me, (26:27).
then I will walk in fury against you, and I, even I, will punish you sevenfold for your sins. (26:28).
You will eat the flesh of your own sons and daughters. (26:29).
I will destroy your high places, cut down your incense altars, and heap your lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of your idols; and My soul will despise you. (26:30).
I will reduce your cities to rubble and lay waste your sanctuaries, and I will refuse to smell the pleasing aroma of your sacrifices. (26:31).
And I will lay waste the land, so that your enemies who dwell in it will be appalled. (26:32).
But I will scatter you among the nations and will draw out a sword after you as your land becomes desolate and your cities are laid waste. (26:33).
Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate, while you are in the land of your enemies. At that time the land will rest and enjoy its Sabbaths. (26:34).
As long as it lies desolate, the land will have the rest it did not receive during the Sabbaths when you lived in it. (26:35).

As for those of you who survive, I will send a faintness into their hearts in the lands of their enemies, so that even the sound of a windblown leaf will put them to flight. And they will flee as one flees the sword, and fall when no one pursues them. (26:36).
They will stumble over one another as before the sword, though no one is behind them. So you will not be able to stand against your enemies. (26:37).
You will perish among the nations, and the land of your enemies will consume you. (26:38).
Those of you who survive in the lands of your enemies will waste away in their iniquity and will decay in the sins of their fathers. (26:39).
But if they will confess their iniquity and that of their fathers in the unfaithfulness that they practiced against Me, by which they have also walked in hostility toward Me— (26:40).
and I acted with hostility toward them and brought them into the land of their enemies— and if their uncircumcised hearts will be humbled and they will make amends for their iniquity, (26:41).
then I will remember My covenant with Jacob and My covenant with Isaac and My covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land. (26:42).

For the land will be abandoned by them, and it will enjoy its Sabbaths by lying desolate without them. And they will pay the penalty for their iniquity, because they rejected My ordinances and abhorred My statutes. (26:43).
Yet in spite of this, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject or despise them so as to destroy them and break My covenant with them; for I am the LORD their God. (26:44).
But for their sake I will remember the covenant with their fathers, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the nations, that I might be their God. I am the LORD.” (26:45).
These are the statutes, ordinances, and laws that the LORD established between Himself and the Israelites through Moses on Mount Sinai. (26:46).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 28:1-68: The same structure of blessings and curses, set out at far greater length.
Deuteronomy 30:1-5: If they take these words to heart among the nations, the LORD will restore them.
2 Chronicles 36:15-21: These curses carried out, and the land keeping its sabbaths while Israel is in Babylon.
Daniel 9:11-14: Daniel names the curse written in the law of Moses as what has come upon them.
Nehemiah 9:26-31: Israel's repeated rebellion and God's repeated patience, laid out as public confession.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָוֹן (ʿavon), Greek: ἀνομία (anomia), Aramaic: עון (ʿawon)
translationNotes.note: Guilt or twistedness; deeper than single acts of sin, denotes ongoing crookedness with its consequences.

Ten thousand; also used idiomatically for 'countless.' Revelation 5:11's 'ten thousands of ten thousands' (myriades myriadon) of angels could be 100 million as a literal floor, though the intent is more naturally read as 'innumerable.'

The chapter runs in five escalating rounds, each opening with a refusal to listen and each raising the penalty sevenfold (26:18, 21, 24, 28). It is a structured warning with stated exits, not a single verdict. Verses 40-45 give the way back at the end of the fifth round.

translationNotes.term: your sky like iron and your land like bronze
translationNotes.note: Sky that yields no rain and ground that will not break, put as two metals. Deuteronomy 28:23 gives the same image with the metals swapped, bronze sky and iron earth. In a rain-fed farming economy this one line is the whole harvest gone.

Bamot are raised open-air worship platforms, and 1 Kings 3:2 notes Israel using them before the temple was built. Chammanim are small incense stands; the word is related to the root for heat or sun. Limestone incense altars of this kind have been excavated at sites in Israel including Megiddo.

The physical sign turned into a description of the inner man. Deuteronomy 10:16 commands Israel to circumcise the foreskin of the heart, Jeremiah 9:26 accuses the nation of being uncircumcised in heart, and Acts 7:51 uses the same charge.

A matsevah is an upright stone set on end, and rows of them have been dug up at Canaanite sites including Gezer and Hazor. Leviticus 26:1 does not ban stones as such; Jacob sets one up and pours oil on it at Genesis 28:18 without rebuke. What the verse forbids is a carved image, a pillar, or a figured paving stone set up to be bowed down to.

translationNotes.term: you will eat the flesh of your own sons and daughters
translationNotes.note: This is a siege warning, and Scripture records it coming true twice. During the Aramean siege of Samaria two women agreed to boil and eat their sons, and one of them brought the case to the king (2 Kings 6:28-29). Lamentations 4:10 says the same of Jerusalem under Babylon. A besieging army did not storm walls if it could avoid the cost; it sat down outside and waited for the food to run out, which took months.

stories.keyTakeaway: God prohibits idols and commands observance of Sabbaths and his sanctuary, promising abundant harvests and military victory if Israel obeys, but describing escalating curses - disease, famine, wild animals, plague, cannibalism, exile, and desolation - if they reject his commands, though he will remember his covenant if they confess their sins and those of their ancestors.

stories.title: ⚖️ Leviticus 27
summaryBullets: Then the LORD said to Moses, (27:1).
“Speak to the Israelites and say to them, ‘When someone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the value of persons, (27:2).
if the valuation concerns a male from twenty to sixty years of age, then your valuation shall be fifty shekels of silver, according to the sanctuary shekel. (27:3).
Or if it is a female, then your valuation shall be thirty shekels. (27:4).
And if the person is from five to twenty years of age, then your valuation for the male shall be twenty shekels, and for the female ten shekels. (27:5).
Now if the person is from one month to five years of age, then your valuation for the male shall be five shekels of silver, and for the female three shekels of silver. (27:6).
And if the person is sixty years of age or older, then your valuation shall be fifteen shekels for the male and ten shekels for the female. (27:7).
But if the one making the vow is too poor to pay the valuation, he is to present the person before the priest, who shall set the value according to what the one making the vow can afford. (27:8).
If he vows an animal that may be brought as an offering to the LORD, any such animal given to the LORD shall be holy. (27:9).
He must not replace it or exchange it, either good for bad or bad for good. But if he does substitute one animal for another, both that animal and its substitute will be holy. (27:10).
But if the vow involves any of the unclean animals that may not be brought as an offering to the LORD, the animal must be presented before the priest. (27:11).
The priest shall set its value, whether high or low; as the priest values it, the price will be set. (27:12).
If, however, the owner decides to redeem the animal, he must add a fifth to its value. (27:13).
Now if a man consecrates his house as holy to the LORD, then the priest shall value it either as good or bad. The price will stand just as the priest values it. (27:14).
But if he who consecrated his house redeems it, he must add a fifth to the assessed value, and it will belong to him. (27:15).
If a man consecrates to the LORD a parcel of his land, then your valuation shall be proportional to the seed required for it — fifty shekels of silver for every homer of barley seed. (27:16).
If he consecrates his field during the Year of Jubilee, the price will stand according to your valuation. (27:17).

But if he consecrates his field after the Jubilee, the priest is to calculate the price in proportion to the years left until the next Year of Jubilee, so that your valuation will be reduced. (27:18).
And if the one who consecrated the field decides to redeem it, he must add a fifth to the assessed value, and it shall belong to him. (27:19).
If, however, he does not redeem the field, or if he has sold it to another man, it may no longer be redeemed. (27:20).
When the field is released in the Jubilee, it will become holy, like a field devoted to the LORD; it becomes the property of the priests. (27:21).
Now if a man consecrates to the LORD a field he has purchased, which is not a part of his own property, (27:22).
then the priest shall calculate for him the value up to the Year of Jubilee, and the man shall pay the assessed value on that day as a sacred offering to the LORD. (27:23).
In the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to the one from whom it was bought — the original owner of the land. (27:24).
Every valuation will be according to the sanctuary shekel, twenty gerahs to the shekel. (27:25).
But no one may consecrate a firstborn of the livestock, because a firstborn belongs to the LORD. Whether it is an ox or a sheep, it is the LORD’s. (27:26).

But if it is among the unclean animals, then he may redeem it according to your valuation and add a fifth of its value. If it is not redeemed, then it shall be sold according to your valuation. (27:27).
Nothing that a man sets apart to the LORD from all he owns — whether a man, an animal, or his inherited land — can be sold or redeemed; everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD. (27:28).
No person set apart for destruction may be ransomed; he must surely be put to death. (27:29).
Thus any tithe from the land, whether from the seed of the land or the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD; it is holy to the LORD. (27:30).
If a man wishes to redeem part of his tithe, he must add a fifth to its value. (27:31).
Every tenth animal from the herd or flock that passes under the shepherd’s rod will be holy to the LORD. (27:32).

He must not inspect whether it is good or bad, and he shall not make any substitution. But if he does make a substitution, both the animal and its substitute shall become holy; they cannot be redeemed.’” (27:33).
These are the commandments that the LORD gave to Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai. (27:34).

Judges 11:30-39: Jephthah's vow and what came of it.
1 Samuel 1:11: Hannah vows to give her son to the LORD for all the days of his life.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵרֶם (ḥerem), Greek: ἀνάθεμα (anathema), Aramaic: חרם (ḥerem)
translationNotes.note: Something irrevocably given over to God, often destroyed; cannot be redeemed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿaser), Greek: δεκάτη (dekatē), Aramaic: מעשר (maʿasar)
translationNotes.note: A tenth part dedicated to God, from crops or herds.
The smallest Hebrew weight unit; twenty gerahs equal one shekel (Exodus 30:13). Approximately half a gram in modern measure.

Every 50th year, after seven sabbatical-year cycles (Leviticus 25). Land returned to original families, Hebrew slaves were freed, and debts cancelled; a structural reset of social and economic inequality. The 'year of the Lord's favor' Jesus proclaims in Luke 4:19 draws directly on jubilee language from Isaiah 61.

Both a weight (about 0.4 oz / 11 g) and a currency unit. In Old Testament economy a common laborer earned roughly half a shekel per month, so the 20 shekels paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28) was about three years of wages. The temple tax was half a shekel (Exodus 30:13); in New Testament reckoning that equaled two denarii / two days' wages.

A fixed price list for redeeming a person vowed to the LORD: fifty shekels for a man aged twenty to sixty, thirty for a woman, twenty and ten for those aged five to twenty, five and three for infants, fifteen and ten for the elderly (27:3-7). At about 11.4 grams a shekel, fifty shekels is roughly 570 grams of silver. Verse 8 lets the priest set a lower figure for anyone who cannot pay.

The largest dry measure, ten ephahs, about 220 liters or a little over six bushels; the word shares its consonants with chamor, a donkey, and a homer is reckoned as a donkey's load. Ezekiel 45:11 fixes the ephah and the bath each at a tenth of it. Leviticus 27:16 prices land by the seed it takes to sow, fifty shekels of silver per homer of barley.

The flock was counted out through a narrow gate while the shepherd touched every tenth animal with his staff to mark it for the tithe (27:32). The owner is forbidden to look them over and pick, or to swap a marked animal for a worse one. Jeremiah 33:13 and Ezekiel 20:37 both use the same picture.

stories.keyTakeaway: God instructs Moses on how to value dedicated persons, animals, houses, and land if someone makes a vow to the LORD, with specific redemption rules and prohibitions on substitution. Tithes of land produce and livestock are declared holy to the LORD and cannot be redeemed or exchanged.

intro:
Leviticus (Hebrew: Vayikra, "And He called") was written by Moses during Israel's encampment at Mount Sinai, traditionally dated to 1445 BC, in the second year after the Exodus from Egypt (c. 1446 BC). After the Tabernacle was completed at the foot of Sinai, the nation remained encamped there for roughly another month before resuming the wilderness journey. The historical setting is the Sinai Peninsula in the early Late Bronze Age, with the Israelites organized as a nomadic camp around the newly constructed Tabernacle. Egypt's 18th Dynasty continued to dominate the broader ancient Near East to the west, with the Mitanni kingdom to the northeast. Moses, the prophet, lawgiver, and leader who had led the nation out of Egyptian slavery, composed the book in real time as he received instruction from God. Jesus and the apostles attribute the Pentateuch, including Leviticus, to Moses (Mark 12:26, Luke 24:44, John 5:46, Romans 10:5).

Leviticus is the third book of the Pentateuch (the five books of Moses). Its Hebrew name Vayikra comes from the opening word of the book, meaning "And He called"; the English title "Leviticus" comes from the Greek Septuagint translation Leuitikon (3rd century BC), via the Latin Vulgate, meaning "pertaining to the Levites." Hebrew manuscript fragments of Leviticus were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 2nd and 1st centuries BC.
